#7492. The Independent Journalism Atlas looks at “wells” and “springs” in news deserts

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

What do we mean when we talk about news deserts?

The term has become a shorthand for areas devoid of local news coverage. But a new essay from the Independent Journalism Atlas recalls that when Penny Abernathy popularized the term through her research, she used it to describe a more nuanced picture:

Things grow in a desert, she told Medill’s Tim Franklin in 2024, just not as abundantly. Asked why she didn’t say “news vacuum,” she answered, “There’s news; it’s just not necessarily the quality and the quantity of what you would find elsewhere.” RELATED ARTICLEFrom bad to worse: 2026 is shaping up to be “a super El Niño year for local news”Sophie CulpepperOctober 13, 2026To show what information can look like in news deserts, the Independent Journalism Atlas — an initiative that aims to “[document] independent creators who inform, educate, and advance public knowledge outside traditional media structures,” cofounded by Liz Kelly Nelson, Justin Bank, and 2025 Nieman Fellow Ryan Kellett — took a closer look at 46 of the 238 news desert counties identified in this year’s State of Local News report from Medill. RELATED ARTICLEMany people who live in “local news deserts” don’t feel deprived of local news, study findsLaura Hazard OwenFebruary 10, 2026“Look at the ground and news moves like water,” writes Bank. “It doesn’t stop at a county line. It runs off the surface, sinks underground and comes up wherever someone digs.” The team found that “in more places than the desert map shows, someone has picked up a shovel.” (That might help explain why people who live in news deserts don’t feel deprived of local news.) The team identifies a few patterns in how information looks and travels in news deserts, including “surface” information, wells, and springs. Posts from the local sheriff, weather alerts, and obituaries from the funeral home are all examples of “surface” information that “runs off,” Bank writes, typically telling you what happened without telling you why. Wells are newsrooms that form when a local paper shutters. The team points to the Anaconda Weekly Review in Deer Lodge County, Montana, as an example of a well appearing in a county Medill identified as a news desert. Springs, meanwhile, are “harder to spot” than wells because they’re smaller and more ad hoc. The Independent Journalism Atlas applies this label to efforts like the Gallatin County Board Illinois Unofficial Facebook page, which livestreams the board’s public meetings and posts its agendas. The team also paid attention to coverage of news deserts by outlets in neighboring counties. They found high school sports are often a gateway to coverage, pointing to a channel covering southern Illinois high school sports that interviewed the principal in Harrisburg, the seat of Saline County, another news desert county. RELATED ARTICLEUniversities are mapping where local news outlets are still thriving — and where gaps persistCorey HutchinsJanuary 16, 2025In recent years, efforts to “map” local news through different lenses have proliferated. The Independent Journalism Atlas is one such effort, focused on news creators. A better understanding of information sources in news deserts matters, Bank argues, because “you can’t tend a basin you haven’t mapped.” Read the full essay here.

#7491. Hearst is working with creators to execute original content and brand deals on the fly

Hearst Communications has a long history of working alongside influencers, and it is bringing that effort into the current phase of the creator economy. A new venture called Hearst Creator Studios combines elements of a talent agency with the structure of a creator network to establish a unit that can deliver original content and branded media.

According to Adweek, Hearst’s new venture will be active across five of its editorial brands, including Cosmopolitan, Elle, and MotorTrend. More than 50 creators are involved, and Hearst is splitting them into two groups. So-called “creators at large” will be contracted to produce content, including at least seven original series. The rest of the creators will be “friends of the brand” who will be plugged into an internal, searchable platform that can be accessed by producers and brands.

Though Hearst is nearly 140 years old, it has never been shy about incorporating digital creators into its editorial brands. Its attempts to turn on that pipeline have evolved alongside the creator economy. A decade ago, Hearst invested in multi-channel networks to gain access to the creator lineups assembled therein. In 2020, its U.K. arm established an “influence network” meant to increase its social media presence. Other Hearst experiments have involved original programming, TikTok integrations, and Reddit-esque upvotes.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

Recently, brands have discovered an exciting new way to harness social media influence: Creator programs. That’s the name given to in-house networks that turn popular creators into brand spokespeople. After companies like Home Depot pioneered the concept, brands like Nat Geo have applied it to the realm of editorial content.

That being said, Hearst Magazines EVP and Global Chief Revenue Officer Lisa Ryan Howard told Adweek that the company’s Creator Studios is not a creator program. Instead, editors-in-chief handpick creator partners and appoint talent managers to work alongside those creators’ reps.

The result is a venture that operates most similarly to a talent agency. “Marketers want this because they want a curatorial eye on the creators,” Howard said, “as well as a one-stop shop.”

The early output from Hearst Creator Studios includes The Feelings Department, which comes from creators Izzy Perez and Emma Fuente and hits Cosmopolitan accounts in November. The plan is to increase the program’s output in 2027, when the 30-plus brands in Hearst’s editorial portfolio will gain access to a burgeoning network of creator partners.

#7490. Google Makes Gemini 4 Hydrogen The Default Model In AI Mode via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

Identify practical ways to improve location visibility in AI-generated answers and recommendations.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

Invalid traffic on AI Max search doubled to 5.28%. Get the channel-by-channel retail benchmarks before Black Friday.

Learn how to prioritize page fixes, check agent access and measure readiness for your 2027 SEO plan.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

Webinar: 9 AI Workflows For Better Content. Nov 18, 2 PM ET.

Google made Gemini 4 Hydrogen the default model in AI Mode for all users and uses it for the hardest AI Overview questions, two days into a core update.

Google made Gemini 4 Hydrogen the default model in AI Mode for all users worldwide, starting today. Sites that track how often AI Mode cites them now have a new model to account for.

In an X thread announcing the change, Robby Stein, VP of Product for Google Search, said Hydrogen is also “being used for your hardest questions in AI Overviews.” Google’s Search post says the model is available globally in Search for all users.

The switch came two days into the November core update, which was still rolling out as of 2:05 p.m. ET today.

The Search post says Hydrogen is able to handle multi-part inquiries, inquiries that contain typos, highly specific inquiries, and follow commands more thoroughly than previous versions of Search.

The post from Search says that Hydrogen also allows for better query fan-out. Query fan-out refers to how Search simultaneously executes multiple queries across each of the subtopics of an inquiry. According to the post, the result is what Google calls “connecting you to a broader range of helpful links than before,” and this includes websites which users may have never stumbled upon themselves. Stein’s thread says that the fan-out improvements result in showing more links to the web. Neither the post nor Stein’s thread provide counts for links or sites.

The post references more visual aids in answers through use of images, structured responses, comparison tables and additional customized tools available to users; additionally, the answers provided will be more nuanced in all languages supported by AI Mode.

The last default change I covered was at I/O back in May when Gemini 3.5 Flash became the global default for AI Mode for everyone. Neither the Search post nor Stein’s post said what Hydrogen replaced.

Stein’s thread has Hydrogen handling the hardest AI Overview questions but doesn’t say which questions count as hardest or what answers the rest. The Search post doesn’t mention AI Overviews.

Google made Gemini 3 the default model for AI Overviews globally in January. At the time, I noted that Google had described plans to send complex questions to Gemini 3 and simpler ones to faster models, and hadn’t said whether that would apply to AI Overviews.

Citation data you pull for AI Mode or AI Overviews this month now spans a model change on Nov. 12. The change applies to AI Mode’s default answers and to the hardest AI Overview questions.

Nov. 12 falls inside the core update window, which began Nov. 10. Logging both dates lets you compare your tracking data before and after each one, rather than reading this month as a single change.

Google’s claim that there are more links doesn’t include figures. You can check how it applies to your site by looking at the citation and referral numbers in your own reports.

Although the Search Status Dashboard shows that the November core update is rolling out, its completion date will be logged as the second date, after Nov. 12.

You should watch for an announcement from Google on which AI Overview questions are classified as hardest so you can see how much of your AI Overview tracking will reflect the change.

Follow on YouTube. Matt G. Southern is the Senior News Writer at Search Engine Journal, where he’s covered Google, SEO, ...

#7489. “A gross abuse of Meta’s power”: California senator Adam Schiff tells Meta to scrap its new terms of service

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

Democratic Senator Adam Schiff of California is urging Meta not to implement its forthcoming commercial terms on November 20, his office announced Tuesday.

In a letter sent to Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, Schiff called on the company to respond by Monday, November 2 with the specific steps it will take to address user concerns.

“Forcing publishers to choose between surrendering their off-platform IP or forfeiting a primary channel of public communication is a gross abuse of Meta’s power as a powerful platform with critical access to consumers,” Schiff wrote. “Meta must not nullify federal IP protections and fair market competition through the unilateral insertion of fine print into terms of service contracts.”

Specifically, Schiff told Meta that it should “provide explicit guarantees that external technical boundaries like paywalls and robots.txt protocols will be fully respected.”

RELATED ARTICLEMeta delays rollout of terms that would allow broad scraping of news sites. Legal experts are still skeptical.Hanaa' TameezOctober 26, 2026“Meta’s verbal assurances that it will not supersede robots.txt files, which are voluntary server flags, do not appear to constitute enforceable legal protections,” Schiff wrote. “Without the insertion of specific language codifying Meta’s policy to respect robots.txt signals into the latest contractual terms, users lack any reliable means by which to protect their content.”

Schiff’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Schiff is the latest elected official in the United States to raise concerns about Meta’s commercial terms, which have now drawn bipartisan criticism. On Friday, Republican Senator Marsha Blackburn of Tennessee said that the terms “indicate Meta is attempting to exploit American creators and businesses by granting itself sweeping authority to scrape content from any website associated with Facebook and Instagram business accounts.”

The terms were previously set to take effect on October 30. Because the terms offered no way to opt out, news of them set off an outcry from news publishers, politicians, and press associations on both sides of the Atlantic. Meta then delayed the effective date of its new terms of service for business accounts to November 20.

On Tuesday, a coalition of Norwegian news publishers sued Meta over the terms and is asking the Oslo District Court to block the terms from going into effect. The legal action, led by the Norwegian Media Companies Association, is the first known lawsuit filed against Meta over its commercial terms.

“We are extending the effective date of our updated Commercial Terms and Self-Serve Ad Terms to November 20 to allow more time for us to explain to our partners and stakeholders what’s changing and what’s not — including how Meta uses web crawlers and the fact that content owners will still be able to use robots.txt to signal preferences,” a Meta spokesperson told Nieman Lab in a statement Friday.

A Meta spokesperson said on October 17 that the company revised the language because it “wasn’t clear in the initial consolidation of terms that robots.txt preferences are respected. News sites, like all other content owners, still have the ability to disable the crawler via robots.txt flags. That has been the case, and it has not changed.”

As of October 27, Meta has made no other changes to the terms aside from the implementation date. No version of the terms includes language about respecting robots.txt preferences.

#7487. Top 50 Most Viewed YouTube Channels Worldwide • Week Of 11/15/2026

[Editor’s Note: Tubefilter Charts is a weekly rankings column from Tubefilter with data provided by GospelStats. It’s exactly what it sounds like; a top number ranking of YouTube channels based on statistics collected within a given time frame. Check out all of our Tubefilter Charts with new installments every week right here.]

Scroll down for this week’s Tubefilter Chart. 👇

We have a new #1 channel in the Global Top 50. Fitu K Kitu picked up 1.19 billion weekly views, a sum that accounts for nearly two-thirds of the channel’s lifetime traffic. Talk about a hot start! Not even chart regulars like T-Series and MrBeast could keep up with Fitu K Kitu’s face.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

Elsewhere in the ranking, a one-time collaborator of MrBeast’s is making waves on his own. One of Latin America’s biggest creators has taken advantage of spooky season while tying in a cultural phenomenon that has had a consistent presence within our charts.

MrBeast isn’t involved in Vigevani’s biggest video of 2026, but a creepy clown is. After claiming to purchase the clown on the dark web, Vigevani used it as the primary prop in a multi-part series that drew inspiration from the smash-hit, YouTube-born franchise Backrooms.

Vigevani dropped his Backrooms-inspired series in the middle of spooky season, and that approach paid off. The ninth installment of the series, which arrived on November 11, was particular popular. It already has nearly 40 million views, and Vigevani has called it his biggest video of the year.

The culmination of Vigevani’s clown serial pushed him up to 27th place in the Global Top 50. He collected 413.1 million weekly views, increasing his YouTube traffic by 28% week-over-week in the process.

English-speaking consumers might think that clown horror is so ten years ago. Back in 2016, a viral clown craze turned into a veritable panic in the days surrounding Halloween. That experience convinced many that clowns are too creepy to belong at children’s parties.

In Latin America, however, clown content still has legs. One of the biggest channels in the region is El Payaso Plim Plim, a clown who isn’t afraid to remain kid-friendly. We’ve had regular Plim Plim sightings in our charts for years, and that trend has continued into 2026. There hasn’t been a week over the past six months in which Plim Plim has collected fewer than 250 million views.

Vigevani has found a clever way to apply that interest in clowns to a more adult audience. By leaning into the inherent horror of pale faces and colorful makeup, Vigevani has revived a decade-old craze and picked up tens of millions of views in the process.

I doubt Plim Plim, who appeals to young children, would approve of Vigevani’s recharacterization of clowns. But that’s what happens when you get your clown on the dark web — you don’t always get what you pay for.

#7486. Creators who show their sources build trust, survey finds

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

Journalist-led research found audiences increased trust when news videos identified their sources, such as government documents and interviews.

RELATED ARTICLETwo-thirds of news influencers are men — and most have never worked for a news organizationSarah ScireNovember 18, 2024About one in five U.S. adults regularly gets their news from news creators on social media platforms, but it can be difficult for audiences to suss out which personalities to trust amid an avalanche of misinformation, hot takes, and polarizing content.

New research spearheaded by a team of journalists and political scientists shows that giving audiences a peek into the reporting process can help bolster their trust in the news.

Proof News, a nonprofit newsroom focused on tech accountability, in collaboration with researchers at the French university Sciences Po, shared social news videos with 2,000 U.S. adults to measure their perceptions of trustworthiness. Participants were randomly assigned one of Proof’s yet-to-be-published short-form news videos.

Some participants viewed videos with labels describing the sources, others saw videos with labels describing the newsroom’s ethical standards, and some saw videos without a label. The Sources labels appeared on cards embedded at the end of the video, like a credits reel, or were placed into the video description, the text accompanying the video.

Participants then rated the videos on various trust metrics. We found that labeling videos did increase trust — particularly a label that described the video sources in the description and, to a slightly lesser extent, a label describing newsroom standards in the credits.

This effect was particularly prominent among survey respondents who identified as Democrats or reported having high trust in science. Those groups, when shown the sourcing label in the description of a general news video, reported higher assessments of transparency and trust in the journalist.

There were fewer statistically significant increases in trust metrics with labels for text articles, but Sally Lehrman, founder of The Trust Project, said the findings were still intriguing.

“I’m excited to see the results,” Lehrman said. “Methods and references really do resonate…People are asking, where did the journalist get this information, and how can I trust it.”

As audiences increasingly turn to social media for news, there is a growing public discussion about how trustworthy creators are, especially when it comes to disclosing their funding and relationships. In January, The Wall Street Journal wrote about corporate and foreign interests using influencers to push agendas. In August, The Washington Post reported that the Pentagon secretly hired conservative military veterans with large online audiences to amplify Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s messaging, and a New York Times investigation revealed online influencers received funding from political campaigns without disclosing the connection in their videos.

Some creators have begun trying to distinguish themselves from this type of behavior through their own disclosure efforts.

RELATED ARTICLEWith Local News International, Dave Jorgenson becomes his own TikTok guyNeel DhaneshaSeptember 9, 2025Journalist and creator Dave Jorgenson, who has nearly 1 million followers across TikTok, YouTube, and Instagram, has started publishing a transparency report on his website, Local News International, revealing his sources of funding alongside his editorial standards.

Ultimately, he thinks disclosures of political funding should no longer be voluntary but mandatory. “Platforms should be regulating themselves,” Jorgenson said in an interview. “You can’t really force that unless there are laws.”

Proof used Jorgenson’s ethics and transparency statement as a model for the newsroom standards label in video testing and found that it increased viewers’ trust in the news outlet and the likelihood that they would share a general news story.

New York City is already considering disclosure requirements in the wake of revelations in the Columbia Journalism Review that exposed the inner workings of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s connections with influencers. The author of the article, Anya Schiffrin, a senior lecturer at Columbia University’s School of International and Public Affairs, testified at a September city council meeting that creator relationships — both paid and unpaid — should be disclosed to viewers.

“It’s important for democracy that we have standards,” Schiffrin said.

RELATED ARTICLEProof News is Julia Angwin’s attempt to bring the scientific method to investigative journalismNeel DhaneshaMarch 21, 2024Proof News, which launched in 2024, pioneered an Ingredients label that takes cues from the scientific method and names the journalists’ hypothesis, sources, limitations, and the story’s findings.

To test whether the label worked to increase viewer trust for short-form vertical videos, we stripped down the Ingredients label to a bullet list of sources followed by an asterisk denoting the reporting limitations. The survey showed the label had a consistent positive effect when placed in the video description, the text box that is often located under the video.

The team also tested how labels performed on online text news articles. The survey showed 1,600 U.S. participants original, unpublished Proof News stories without a label, with a Proof Ingredients label, a label modeled after the Trust Project that described the reporting process, and a label describing newsroom standards.

There were fewer statistically significant increases in trust metrics with the print labels. The most significant findings were an increase in perception of transparency when the reporting process label was used on a polarizing story and an investigative story.

One possible explanation for the differing results between labeling video and text articles is the “ergonomics” of the medium, said Damien Bol, a professor at the Center for Political Research at Sciences Po who helped lead the survey design and data analysis.

“When reading a text, for example, people can quickly skim through it or skip parts of it, whereas a video forces them to follow the story second by second, even when watching at double speed,” Bol said. Different formats, Bol said, shape the “experience of consuming a news story.”

Earlier this month, Julia Angwin, an author of this article, hosted a private convening of creators at Harvard Kennedy School’s Shorenstein Center on Media, Politics and Public Policy to discuss creating shared standards that could be conveyed through a label or other public statement.

The group of 30 leading content creators from news, science communication, education, history, and other evidence-based fields discussed how they could distinguish their work by signaling to viewers their commitment to standards that could include disclosing funding sources and the use of artificial intelligence. Creator-led efforts to bring this to fruition are ongoing.

San Diego-based journalist Lisa Remillard, who has more than 4 million followers on her TikTok channel “The News Girl,” said that making videos with verified facts can feel like a small club. But if she can’t independently confirm something, she’s “not putting that out there.”

Remillard’s audience appears to appreciate transparency. Earlier this year, she published a video describing her editorial standards — and was richly rewarded for it. “I think clearly defining those ethics and standards resonated with my audience and gave them a reason to want to financially support my work,” Remillard said.

Jessica Yellin, the founder of the political podcast, YouTube channel, and social media brand “News Not Noise,” has also called for news creators to voluntarily sign a Creator Constitution, agreeing to journalistic standards such as citing sources, fixing errors, and disclosing financial relationships.

She said labeling sources is about the “signal.” Even if audiences don’t take the time to digest every word, Yellin observed, “It’s the act of showing it that matters.”

Julia Angwin is the founder of Proof News and the founding director of the Independent Media + Audience Project at the Shorenstein Center on Media, Politics and Public Policy at Harvard Kennedy School. Annie Gilbertson is managing editor of Proof News. Rina Palta is editor-at-large at Proof News and senior data scientist at the Independent Media + Audience Project.

Julia Angwin is the founder of Proof News and the founding director of the Independent Media + Audience Project at the Shorenstein Center on Media, Politics and Public Policy at Harvard Kennedy School. Google Ads introduces an Invalid Traffic Overview Card showing estimated savings, post-billing credits, and campaign-level reports. Here's what advertisers need to know.

Google Ads is rolling out a new Invalid Traffic Overview Card that shows advertisers how much invalid activity its systems filter before billing, along with credits issued after billing.

Until now, advertisers had to look across campaign reports and monthly billing statements to find that information. The new card brings those figures into one view, with additional reporting available by day and campaign.

Ginny Marvin, Google Ads Liaison, announced the rollout on LinkedIn and shared more details in the latest Ads Decoded newsletter.

The global rollout began this week, and the feature is also available in Search Ads 360 for Google Ads accounts.

Advertisers can find the new card on the Google Ads Overview page, under the Campaigns tab.

Google has long used automated systems and manual reviews to filter invalid ad interactions, including bot activity, accidental clicks, and attempts to artificially inflate traffic.

Most of that activity is caught before billing, so advertisers aren’t charged for those interactions.

The new card includes three reporting areas:

Clicking “View details” opens a daily trend chart and campaign table. Advertisers can also access the monthly invoices where credits were applied.

The estimated savings figure is the main addition to this information. Advertisers could already review invalid click metrics, but those reports didn’t show the estimated dollar amount Google had prevented from being charged.

According to Marvin, Google’s systems catch the majority of invalid traffic before it reaches an advertiser’s invoice.

Google Ads locks standard campaign metrics at month-end to match billing records. If Google detects more invalid traffic after that, any credits issued won’t change the Cost or CPA figures in the main Campaigns table.

Advertisers who want to see those adjustments reflected in their performance metrics can use the Invalid Activity Credit: Search & PMax report.

Available in Report editor, it includes 10 columns, such as Adjusted cost and Adjusted cost / conv. Credits are attributed to the dates the ads originally ran, even when Google issued them later.

This gives advertisers a way to review Search and Performance Max costs with post-billing invalid activity credits factored in, without relying solely on the standard Campaigns table.

The campaign-level breakdowns should make it easier to see where Google is filtering invalid activity, although the estimated savings figures will need some context.

A campaign with significantly more spend could show higher estimated savings simply because it’s generating more traffic. Comparing those dollar amounts alone won’t necessarily tell advertisers which campaigns have greater traffic quality concerns.

There’s also a limit to what the numbers can tell us. The card reflects activity Google’s systems have identified as invalid, but it doesn’t establish how much fraudulent traffic may have gone undetected.

For lead generation accounts, invalid traffic reporting won’t necessarily explain why fake or low-quality leads are continuing to come in.

Marvin addressed this in the Ads Decoded newsletter: Google’s systems can filter invalid ad interactions, but bad leads can still come from legitimate clicks or submissions that never originated from an ad.

An account could have relatively little invalid traffic reported in Google Ads and still struggle with lead quality. Advertisers dealing with those issues will need to compare the reporting against their CRM data rather than assuming Google’s invalid traffic figures tell the whole story.

Featured image: Primakov (screenshot from Google Ads Decoded Newsletter) / Shutterstock

#7482. Substack management firm Brigade snapped up by Hollywood’s Entertainment 360

Entertainment 360, the Hollywood talent and literary management company that reps celebrities like Margot Robbie and Julianne Moore, has acquired Brigade, a digital talent firm that specializes in Substack writers and podcasters.

As part of the deal, Brigade founder Max Stein will join Entertainment 360 as a Partner. He’ll bring with him Brigade’s team of managers and the firm’s ~40 clients, all of whom will keep their current representatives, he told The New York Times.

Among those clients are notable Substack writers Leandra Medine Cohen (a well-known fashion maven) and Emily Sundberg, who writes daily business newsletter Feed Me, as well as podcast host/creative consultant Chris Black and celebrity stylist Danielle Goldberg.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

Hollywood’s interest in creators has been the big buzz for a while, but that interest tends to zero in on moviemakers. Brigade’s clients–particularly its Substack contingent–are from other, oft-overlooked disciplines where digital talent and legacy entertainment could mesh.

“I’ve always been drawn to people with a singular point of view, whose work and ambitions don’t fit neatly into one category,” Stein, who got his start in fashion and launched Brigade in 2015, said in a statement. “Our clients have built remarkable careers by following their own taste and instincts, and our job has been to help them turn those ideas into lasting businesses.”

Entertainment 360 Partner Darin Friedman told The Hollywood Reporter that the worlds of digital and legacy entertainment “have collapsed a bit on each other.”

“YouTube is competing with Netflix, and Netflix is buying podcasts, and Disney is wanting to set meetings with comedians who want to develop TV shows,” he added.

In a separate statement, Entertainment 360’s Partners collectively said they’ve noticed “[t]he ways audiences discover and engage with entertainment have changed, and so have the needs of the talent building careers today.”

“Bringing Brigade into 360 expands what we can offer our clients and strengthens our ability to create extraordinary opportunities for artists across an increasingly diverse entertainment landscape,” they added.

Stein, meanwhile, told NYT that Brigade’s digital clients “are still attracted to some of the more legacy things.”

Sundberg took to LinkedIn to offer her own perspective on the deal.

“I’d be nervous if I were one of two groups of people–teams at the giant talent agencies like WME and United Talent Agency who aren’t spending time learning about the economics and opportunities of platforms like Substack; and Substack’s internal ad team, who needs to learn how to work with agencies like Entertainment 360 (and Spur and Amplifier and Alltogether) who already have deep relationships with advertisers,” she said.

Substack might be one step ahead there: As Digiday spotted today, Substack has a new job listing out for a U.S.-based Product Manager of Payments. The role’s description says the manager will handle gifting, retention offers, and improvement to payment and subscription experiences, along with advertising monetization–all with the (presumed) goal of getting creators paid more.

Substack already pumped up newsletter sponsorships earlier this year, debuting Creator Kits to help writers secure brand deals. Other creator-friendly adds to its service include a TikTok-style promo feed and a $20 million Creator Accelerator Fund.

360 and Brigade didn’t disclose financials of their acquisition, but we’re betting they both see potential gold in uniting across largely unexplored territory.

#7481. Vox launches its first app with an eye toward building paid memberships

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

Vox users can watch videos and listen to podcasts in the app, but reading stories requires a paid subscription.

Vox has launched its first mobile application, the publication best known for its explanatory journalism announced Wednesday morning.

Growing membership is a “key priority,” managing editor for audience and membership Bill Carey said. Vox believes launching the app is one way to do that. A Vox membership costs $5 per month, or $60 per year, and offers ad-free versions of podcasts and unlimited access to all of the website’s contents.

RELATED ARTICLEVox is revamping its editorial strategy to redefine what ‘Voxxy’ meansHanaa' TameezNovember 8, 2021Strengthening its relationship to its audience is only becoming more important for Vox. The app launch comes at a time when news publishers are increasingly trying to keep users on their own platforms amid growing preferences for AI summaries, news creators, and industry-wide traffic declines.

“The move toward developing our membership program in the last couple of years has really been about understanding how important it is for us to build more community and to foster that loyalty [of our] audience,” Carey said. “When we were looking at that, it really felt like an app was a good way to continue pointing in that direction.”

Vox isn’t the only news outlet focusing on mobile apps. The Verge — Vox’s former sister publication under Vox Media — named traffic declines as one of the reasons why it plans to launch its own app next year. The Wall Street Journal’s head of digital, Taneth Evans, recently said that the Journal makes its app more useful to users by offering all of its mediums in one place. Evans also said that news publishers “need to give people reasons to open an app beyond simply offering news.”

“Websites will become a service for agents,” Evans said. “Apps are gonna be the thing that humans will connect with.”

Vox declined to provide website traffic numbers, but data from Comscore shows that the website’s unique visitors decreased by 36% year-over-year between September 2025 (7.4 million) and September 2026 (4.8 million). Archived data from SimilarWeb shows the site had 20.8 million visits in September 2021.

“Vox isn’t immune to the larger trends that have led to web traffic declines in recent years, but those only represent a portion of our audience,” Carey said in an email. “Vox is focused on building audience engagement across platforms, with social video views up 86% year-over-year and newsletter audience up 14%.”

“Even if there wasn’t a decline in search traffic, as everyone has been seeing — and we still get members from search — we want to create that relationship with our audience,” publisher and editor-in-chief Swati Sharma said. “People know Vox and they have a relationship with Vox. We have a younger audience that’s on all of these different platforms. I think it is definitely a part of building that relationship ourselves.”

That the app makes all Vox content accessible in one place for current and future members also signals the “un-siloing” of the newsroom overall, Sharma said. Vox currently has 78 editorial employees.

RELATED ARTICLESwati Sharma is leading a new era in Vox’s mission to “explain the world”Hanaa' TameezMay 6, 2021When Sharma, who has helmed Vox.com since 2021, first arrived, she found that Vox’s main mediums (text, audio, and video) “weren’t in service of one another.” The “silos” allowed teams to build their own audiences and products. But while teams discussed story ideas with each other and during editorial meetings, “they all [needed] to go into their creative spaces and find what works for their medium and not be in service of just one larger section.”

That’s changed over the past five years, Sharma said. Each team — text, video, and audio — does a little bit of everything now. Text reporters appear on podcasts and in videos, while podcasters and hosts also write their own newsletters.

“In a lot of newsrooms, there’s one dominant form, and at Vox, there wasn’t. They’re all really important,” Sharma said. “[Senior correspondent] Dylan Scott is on our Unexplainable podcast talking about Alzheimer’s. [Host and editorial director] Astead Herndon does a newsletter and a Substack Live every week, and he does a podcast. That’s the future for us, and that’s where our whole newsroom is moving, where those silos are done and you can basically do everything.”

#7479. Meta pledges to consult publishers before finalizing its new terms

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

Meta will complete “a full consultation” with news industry leaders before implementing its controversial new terms — even if it means another delay, an executive for the social media company announced today.

“We’ve heard publishers’ feedback on our proposed ads and business terms update. We care deeply about our partners and do not plan to make policy changes without a full consultation with industry groups and leaders,” vice president of communications Andy Stone tweeted. “We’re committed to getting this right, and as we expect this consultation could extend beyond November 20, in which case we’d delay implementation of the updated terms. Until then our existing terms remain in place.”

Meta did not answer Nieman Lab’s questions about which news industry groups and leaders Meta plans to consult.

The proposed terms have drawn criticism because they would permit broad scraping of websites “associated with” business accounts, and potentially allow Meta to use that scraped content to train its AI models, with no option to opt out. Last week, Meta announced it would push back implementation of its new terms to November 20 in order to “explain to our partners and stakeholders what’s changing and what’s not — including how Meta uses web crawlers and the fact that content owners will still be able to use robots.txt to signal preferences,” a Meta spokesperson told Nieman Lab. Meta had previously revised its new terms to remove the word “train.” No version of the terms has included language about respecting robots.txt preferences.

Shortly after Stone’s announcement, a Norwegian court blocked Meta’s terms from taking effect on November 20 until the court had assessed their legality, the country’s public broadcaster NRK reported.

“We are satisfied that the court has agreed with us that Meta holds a dominant position in the relevant market and that the new terms are unreasonable,” said Lene Eltvik Vindfeld, MBL’s board chair, in a news release. “We are also pleased that the court recognizes that the alternative is that media companies risk losing control over editorial content built up over many years.”

Since Nieman Lab first reported on the terms on October 15, publishers and politicians around the world have pushed back, filing complaints with national competition authorities, calling on the European Commission to investigate, and writing letters to Meta’s CEO Mark Zuckerberg. Two United States senators — California Democrat Adam Schiff and Tennessee Republican Marsha Blackburn — each separately wrote to Zuckerberg, insisting that the company withdraw the terms as they’re currently written.

“After I raised serious concerns about Meta’s plans to scrape and abuse creators’ content, I am pleased the company is finally acknowledging the concerns of publishers and content creators,” Blackburn said in a statement to Nieman Lab on Wednesday. “While this is a step in the right direction, a vague promise to consult with industry stakeholders and potentially delay implementation is not nearly enough. Meta must commit to meaningful changes that protect the intellectual property rights of American creators, and I will continue holding the company accountable until it does.”

On October 21, the European Publishers Council signed onto a joint letter to the European Commission, asking the Commission to block the terms from taking effect. The letter claims that Meta’s terms violate the Digital Markets Act, a law passed in 2020 to curb the dominance of big tech companies and create fairer competition across the region.

EPC executive director Angela Mills Wade said on Wednesday that the organization has not heard from Meta about its letter or its concerns.

“We welcome Meta’s offer to consult publishers fully, and to delay implementation if necessary,” Mills Wade said in an email to Nieman Lab. “However, that consultation must lead to binding contractual safeguards…Using Meta’s services to reach audiences or advertise should not mean granting wider rights to exploit publishers’ journalism, whether collected from websites or uploaded to its platforms. Publishers must retain control over additional uses of their content, including for AI, and the ability to negotiate licenses and payment.”

This story has been updated to include a statement from Marsha Blackburn.

#7476. What Reddit Reviews Reveals About Your Products via @sejournal, @brentcsutoras

Identify practical ways to improve location visibility in AI-generated answers and recommendations.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

Invalid traffic on AI Max search doubled to 5.28%. Get the channel-by-channel retail benchmarks before Black Friday.

Learn how to prioritize page fixes, check agent access and measure readiness for your 2027 SEO plan.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

Webinar: 9 AI Workflows For Better Content. Nov 18, 2 PM ET.

Spot recurring product complaints and competitor comparisons with Reddit Reviews, then check source comments for context before making marketing decisions.

If Reddit’s taught us anything over the last five years, it’s that people really do care about validating the assumptions that they’re making along their journey. They really want to hear from real users who have actually used something or tried something, what their experience was, even if they don’t know who those users are.

People want to see the questions, complaints, and comparisons that come up when they are deciding what to buy. Reddit Reviews brings those conversations together on one page, giving people another way to find those experiences and click through to the original discussions.

On Nov. 10, Reddit announced the Reviews test with summaries of product conversations, themes about what people like and dislike, commonly compared products, and comments that lead back to their original discussions. Reddit says the initial rollout will reach U.S. users in English on web, iOS, and Android. It covers about 10,000 products across electronics, health and beauty, home and garden, and fashion and apparel. It plans to add products and categories and expand beyond the U.S. during 2027.

That can make research easier to inspect. A shopper can move from a summary to the comment, see the community where it appeared, and follow the details that matter to them. Reddit says some pages will also include images, prices, and purchase links supplied through brand and retailer catalogs. Those details are worth checking, especially when a page’s price or product information does not match the retailer’s current listing.

See also: Why Your Product Feed Is An SEO Asset (And Who Should Own It)

Reddit Reviews can help surface patterns, but there are limitations explained in the page FAQs. A verified purchase is not required; Reddit does not confirm that someone bought or used a product, and AI can miss context. The sentiment display gives a quick view of included conversations, while the detailed comments show what went into it. A review cannot represent every customer or provide an exact percentage.

Before drawing a conclusion from a review about your brand, I would ask: Is the same complaint coming up in different threads? Is the summary missing a condition that changes the recommendation? Are people comparing your product with a competitor for a reason your team has not been tracking? That context is where the useful research is.

A moderator’s concern was raised in the launch discussion about figuring out whether product recommendations come from people with firsthand experience. One commenter said verifying whether book recommendations came from people who had read the books was “already a gigantic challenge.” The moderator’s comment does not measure how Reddit Reviews performs, but it does point to a real trust question for any system summarizing community advice.

See also: The Review Gap: Finding Client Opportunities In Competitor Feedback

I would treat these review pages as another place for brands to listen. Check whether a review exists for the products and categories you care about, compare its summary with the source comments, note the products people consider alongside yours, and check whether the merchant information is current. Then compare recurring questions and objections with what support, product, and research teams already hear.

That can tell you where expectations and experience diverge. It cannot tell you what all customers think, how many people bought, or whether Reviews changed a purchase. Reddit says the initial pages draw from eligible conversations and that businesses cannot pay for product inclusion.

There is no conversion result to claim yet. So, watch how review pages appear in Reddit search, and check the referral and conversion data available on your own site before drawing conclusions about sales.

This is also a reason to make the community conversations themselves better. Give people room to ask real questions, share tradeoffs, and explain what did or did not work. If your team participates, be clear about who you are and help where you are welcome. My earlier piece on Reddit and the purchase journey makes the same point: People use Reddit to validate a decision, and the experience behind the recommendation is what gives that conversation value.

This is why we work with all of our clients to make sure that we’re building a community for them where their users have a place to come and share and talk about their products and their experiences.

When you spot a recurring product problem or a comparison buyers keep making, take it back to the team that can do something with it. That is the kind of information I think marketers can actually use.

#7475. The New York Times is adding more AI features to its Cooking app, and users aren’t thrilled

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

Sometimes, adding just one new ingredient to a stew can ruin the whole thing.11Olives, yecch. And that’s how at least some New York Times readers see its addition of AI features to its popular Cooking app.

Here’s Genevieve Ko, NYT Cooking senior editor and columnist, explaining the new features:

I naïvely assumed A.I. wouldn’t affect my work as a recipe developer and my role at NYT Cooking, where I oversee the editorial side of our recipes and related stories. But as artificial intelligence improved, our product and engineering colleagues saw its potential to help us create features Cooking users wanted.

The Times had previously rolled out AI features aimed at converting volume-based and weight-based measurements (“What’s one cup of bok choy in grams?”) and scaling a recipe up or down to serve more or fewer people. The main new feature is focused on ingredient substitutions.

Say you’re cooking braised white beans and greens with parmesan, NYT Cooking app in hand. But you notice that you’re out of chard and only have spinach. Cooking veterans know that chard is a rough-and-tumble green that has some backbone22There’s a reason one type of chard is known as “perpetual spinach.”, while spinach is a comparative wimp that will wilt the moment you look at it funny. If you need to sub in spinach for chard, how would the recipe change? Would you, for instance, add the spinach later than you would the chard to account for its pathetic stamina? That’s the sort of thing the new AI feature could account for.

Cooking staffers “spent countless hours evaluating sample after sample to get the chatbot answers to closely align with how we would answer as culinary experts,” Ko writes. “We applied the same rigor as we do to editing, grounded in Times standards.”

But because Ko knows that any AI-powered features are likely to be controversial with a Times audience, she spends quite a lot of space addressing potential objections, everything from “the impact of data centers” to “the concentration of power among A.I. companies” and “the risk of A.I. escaping our control.” These features are designed to enable “the tactile physical pleasure of cooking” and getting a “very real, very human creation” on your table.

Broadly speaking, commenters weren’t buying it.

“What a massive disappointment,” wrote Susan from New Jersey. “The internet is full of AI cooking content. I pay you because I prefer mine done by people.”

“This decision misses the mark by such a wide margin it’s baffling,” says Ian from Los Angeles. “And the disclosure just as baffling. It would not be inaccurate to summarize the piece as saying ‘I know doing this is bad and I don’t want to be associated with the bad thing so that’s why we are doing the bad thing.'”

“Nobody wants this, it’s bad for cooking, it’s bad for the NYT,” writes Bill from Pittsburgh. “Wasting a column trying to gaslight yourself and your audience into believing that it’s anything but is an embarrassment and a waste of everyone’s time.”

“PLEASE PLEASE PLEASE DO NOT DO THIS,” says Judah Mann of New York. “Oh, wait, you already did. Ok, I’m out.”

Or as Naomi from California puts it: “I am sad that AI has breached the one online resource I truly love.”

Because I enjoy the irony, I scraped the 171 comments left on the Times’ announcement and asked Codex (running GPT-6.1 Sol, at medium thinking) to do some sentiment analysis. (Twelve of the 171 were comments left by Times staffers; I’m excluding them here.) Roughly 77% of the reader comments were negative about the new AI features, it found, versus 14% positive and the remainder neutral or mixed. Among the biggest categories of complaint: This shouldn’t require AI. AI is destroying the environment. AI is not why I’m paying the Times $390 a year. The adjustments the AI produces are going to be bad.

Dozens of commenters asked for a way to turn off the feature. “No, not at this time,” Ko responded, “though this feature is completely optional to use.” Indeed: Don’t ask AI to substitute your chard and AI won’t substitute your chard.

One consistent thread was that cooking is supposed to present you with difficulties and challenges and the whole point is figuring them out by yourself. “Anyone using AI for cooking has no sense of taste and no desire to work out the intricacies of cooking and baking,” writes Michael King from Brooklyn. “To use AI for recipes is beyond the pale. If you are going to use AI, then just cut to the chase and defenestrate yourself.” Or BJ from North Carolina: “So, you’re telling me that I’m too stupid to figure it out on my own?”

Meanwhile, the few positive comments tended to focus on how the AI feature had, in fact, made dietary substitutions easier for them. “I love the new AI feature because it quickly (and so far) accurately converts recipes to gluten free,” Anne Wagner from Kansas City writes. “I don’t cook for stress relief,” says Andy from San Francisco. “I cook to put dinner on the table. Anything that makes the process a little faster or smoother is welcome.”

#7473. Only 32% of Americans have high confidence that news orgs will report midterm election results accurately, survey finds

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

About six in 10 Americans said they have at least “some” confidence that news organizations will report the upcoming midterm election results accurately, according to a new national survey. But only 32% said they had “quite a bit” or “a great deal” of confidence that journalists would do the job.

In the survey from Medill Local News Initiative and the Alliance for Trust in Media, 37% said they had either “not too much confidence” or “no confidence at all” that news outlets would accurately report the election results.

The survey was completed by a nationally representative sample of 1,057 U.S. adults either online or by telephone earlier this month. The findings echo other national surveys, including a Gallup survey that showed trust in media to report “fully, accurately, and fairly” at 33% — an increase from an all-time low last year.

The Medill/Alliance survey found about half of Americans said they had “not too much confidence” or “no confidence at all” in news outlets to investigate voter fraud claims thoroughly. U.S. President Donald Trump has cast doubt on elections on 70% of days since returning to office — starting with false claims about voter fraud on the first day of his second term.

In another bleak result from the same poll, slightly more survey respondents said journalists manipulate the news for political or commercial purposes than report it accurately. Across the survey, Democrats reported being more confident in (and trusting of) news organizations than Republicans. Nearly 80% of Republicans said journalists try to manipulate the news compared to 38% of independents and 24% of Democrats.

More on the survey, conducted by NORC at the University of Chicago, here.

#7470. 72% Of Worker’s Say Their AI Skills Are Untested – Here’s How PPC Managers Prove Theirs via @sejournal, @gregjarboe

Identify practical ways to improve location visibility in AI-generated answers and recommendations.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

Invalid traffic on AI Max search doubled to 5.28%. Get the channel-by-channel retail benchmarks before Black Friday.

Learn how to prioritize page fixes, check agent access and measure readiness for your 2027 SEO plan.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

Webinar: 9 AI Workflows For Better Content. Nov 18, 2 PM ET.

Turn Google Ads automation decisions into proof of your AI skills by logging overrides, checks, and results that a Skillshop certificate can't show.

If you manage Google Ads accounts, being “good” with AI is expected, but employers probably never checked (or didn’t know how to check) if you are. Being able to show your judgment is a career must if you can, and a risk if you can’t.

New research from CodeSignal surveyed 1,000 U.S. employees and 1,000 U.S. people managers about AI readiness, and two numbers sit side by side in the results. 72% of workers surveyed say their AI skills have never been formally evaluated, yet 69% of managers call AI ability a major or moderate factor in hiring. Indicating that employers are hiring for a skill they mostly don’t measure.

I sent CodeSignal 15 questions about how solid those numbers are and what practitioners should do about them. The written answers were more candid than I expected, including on the obvious conflict of interest of an assessment vendor concluding that nobody assesses anything. Here’s what holds up, what needs a footnote, and what it means for people who run paid search for a living.

Start with what this survey is and isn’t. CodeSignal commissioned two online surveys through Pollfish in September 2026, and both samples were entirely U.S.-based. The company defined knowledge workers by the work they do rather than by job title, meaning people whose jobs run mainly on computers and digital tools. It also didn’t screen out people who skip AI. 12% said they never use it at work.

CodeSignal reports that roles where AI use is required or expected “jumped 78%.” I asked whether that meant percentage points. It doesn’t. It’s a relative increase, self-reported by employees about their own roles, measured across each person’s time in their current job. When respondents started those jobs, 9.4% said AI use was required or expected of them. Today, 16.7% say so.

That’s nearly double. It’s also fewer than one in five.

Paid search people are probably well past that curve already, since automated bidding has been Google’s default recommendation for years. So, the useful question for our field is whether anyone can tell who is using AI well.

See also: From T-Shaped To M-Shaped: The PPC Career Evolution Nobody Is Talking About

62% of employees told CodeSignal they received employer training on how to use AI at work. Only 35% said employer training is where they built the AI skills they actually use.

I asked whether most of that training simply wasn’t about AI, or whether workers weren’t counting it. CodeSignal said neither. The training was specifically about using AI at work, and the company reads the gap as a sign that it wasn’t substantial or specific enough to apply on the job.

The follow-up number is worse. Only about one in four trained workers said they can apply most or all of their employer’s AI training. The other 74% apply some, very little, or none of it. Run that against the full sample and roughly 46% of all workers got AI training they can’t fully use. When CodeSignal asked what gets in the way, employees named lack of time, training that doesn’t fit their role, and lack of access to relevant training.

So, where are people learning? The question allowed multiple answers, which is why the figures don’t add up to 100. Free resources people found on their own led at 46%, followed by trial and error on the job at 39%, and employer training at 35%. Colleagues came in at 22%, and courses people paid for themselves at 12%.

Tigran Sloyan, CodeSignal’s co-founder and CEO, said, “Companies are buying AI courses or building their own, but if most workers are going elsewhere to learn, you have to wonder if that training is actually helping.”

Paid search has worked this way for a long time. Plenty of PPC managers learned bidding by watching their own accounts and reading practitioners on LinkedIn and X. What has changed is that the thing they now learn by trial and error is the ad platform’s own AI, and each error is paid for out of a client’s budget.

72% of workers say their AI skills have never been formally evaluated, but 66% say the same about their skills in general. That’s a six-point gap.

I asked CodeSignal whether the real story is that companies don’t assess much of anything, and AI just makes that visible. The answer began with “Yes, exactly.” Companies have long made people decisions on proxies such as resumes, job titles, tenure, and manager impressions. CodeSignal’s argument is that those were always weak signals, and they get costly when roles shift in months. More than six in ten managers in the survey said they make people decisions based on assumptions rather than reliable data.

This bothers me more in paid media than almost anywhere else. We measure campaigns to the decimal point. We argue about attribution windows, incrementality tests, and conversion lag. Then we judge the people running those campaigns with a once-a-year “meets expectations.” For a discipline built on measurement, that’s a strange double standard, and AI is making it harder to defend.

CodeSignal says the hiring side already shows the strain. When AI fluency is a criterion nobody has measured, people get judged on what’s easy to see, such as who is most visible or sounds most confident, instead of on the quality of their work.

Anyone who has sat through an agency pitch knows how that plays out. The person who says the automation will figure it out can sound more fluent than the person who spent the afternoon reading search terms and adding negatives. Only one of them is protecting the budget.

“A resume is a story someone tells about their skills,” Sloyan said. “The work is the proof. Right now, most companies are making their biggest decisions about people based on the story.”

See also: PPC Automation Layering: How Smart Advertisers Combine Automation With Strategy

I asked CodeSignal to separate “AI fluency” from AI literacy and prompt-writing, because those terms get used as if they were the same thing. The company drew the lines this way. Literacy means understanding what AI is. Prompt-writing is a tactic. Fluency means knowing what to delegate to AI, checking and correcting its output, and recognizing when not to use it at all.

That is the best short job description for a modern PPC manager I’ve read this year.

Map it onto a Google Ads account, and each part becomes something you can point to. Delegation is deciding which campaigns get Smart Bidding, which conversion actions you feed it, and what budget it gets to learn on. Checking is reading the search terms, placements, and automatically created assets that the system produces, then correcting what’s wrong. Knowing when not to use AI is the judgment call that rarely shows up in a dashboard. That might mean holding back a campaign with too little conversion data, or keeping a human hand on ad copy in a regulated category.

None of that is visible in a certificate. All of it is visible in the account.

See also: The Conversion Setup Errors That Break Smart Bidding

I also asked CodeSignal to critique its own product category. What can a timed, simulated assessment not tell you about whether someone uses AI well on the job? The company answered that an assessment is only as useful as what it was designed and validated to measure. To understand how someone performs over time, it said, you need to look at their actual work.

That answer applies just as well to the credential most PPC people already hold. Google’s AI-Powered Performance Ads Certification on Skillshop is free, and third-party study guides describe it as a timed, 50-question exam. It’s worth taking, because it teaches how Google wants its AI campaign types used. But it’s written by the platform whose recommendations a good PPC manager sometimes overrides. Passing it shows you know Google’s playbook. It can’t show the afternoon you decided not to follow it, or what happened to cost per acquisition when you didn’t.

Then there’s the conflict of interest. CodeSignal sells assessments, and its survey concludes that skills aren’t being assessed. I asked how readers should weigh that, and what finding cut against its business.

The company said its interest in skills is the reason it commissioned the study. Then it volunteered a number that does cut the other way. 82% of employees said their manager understands their skills very or somewhat well. CodeSignal called that knowledge real and valuable. Its caveat is that the knowledge is informal, varies from manager to manager, doesn’t follow people when they change teams, and can’t be compared across a company.

Agency people will recognize that last part. When an account manager moves to another client team, everything their old boss knew about their judgment usually stays behind.

I give CodeSignal credit for offering up the 82%. I’d still want to see the full questionnaire before treating any of these figures as settled, and the company’s launch announcement for its Agentic Skills Intelligence product doesn’t describe the survey method at all. The details above came from its answers to my questions.

CodeSignal’s advice to individual workers was blunt. Saying you use AI for everything doesn’t prove much. Fluency is being able to explain exactly how you use it and, just as important, when you don’t. For a PPC manager, that turns into a short routine.

If you lead a PPC team or run an agency, the company’s advice for a 200-person business with no assessment budget translates well. Start with managers, since most employees think their managers already understand their skills. Then give those managers something more concrete than “meets expectations” by writing down what good AI use looks like for each role on the team. A specialist’s standard might be catching irrelevant search terms within a week. A strategist’s might be deciding when a client’s conversion tracking is clean enough to move to value-based bidding.

Next, look at real account work before training and again after it. A sample of a few accounts per person is enough to see whether anything changed.

Find your self-taught experts, too. With 46% of workers learning from free resources on their own, someone on your team has probably already worked out what the automation gets wrong. Have them show everyone else.

Finally, build training around the work people do every week and give them time to practice. Lack of time was the obstacle employees named first. Track whether people use what they learned, not whether they finished the course. A Skillshop badge is a completion metric, and you’d never let a client judge a campaign on impressions alone.

Sloyan’s version of this is worth quoting. “Training only works when it’s built around the job someone actually does.”

My view is that PPC managers have an advantage most knowledge workers in this survey don’t. Our work already leaves a record. Every bid strategy change, every negative keyword, and every recommendation we dismissed is logged somewhere, with performance data attached.

Most of us treat that record as housekeeping. The managers who turn it into evidence of judgment are the ones who will get promoted while their employers are still figuring out how to measure AI skills at all.
