#7423. ChatGPT Ads Vs. Google Search Ads: What Early Data Shows via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

Identify practical ways to improve location visibility in AI-generated answers and recommendations.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

Invalid traffic on AI Max search doubled to 5.28%. Get the channel-by-channel retail benchmarks before Black Friday.

Learn how to prioritize page fixes, check agent access and measure readiness for your 2027 SEO plan.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

Webinar: 9 AI Workflows For Better Content. Nov 18, 2 PM ET.

ChatGPT competes for ad budgets, but revenue and survey data don't show how much left search. Its ad visits earned less in early data; per dollar is estimated.

This past week, OpenAI rolled out cost-target bidding in its ChatGPT Ads platform. These ads first launched in February. By Aug. 31, OpenAI reported that its ads product had achieved a $1 billion annualized run rate.

The question for a paid search team is whether ChatGPT Ads now compete with Google Search Ads for advertising dollars, and whether the early results make a case for moving some of their budget to ChatGPT Ads.

ChatGPT Ads are competing for advertisers’ budgets. However, the revenue metrics, survey data, and Google’s disclosures I reviewed give no indication of how many dollars have been diverted away from Google Search Ads to ChatGPT Ads.

In terms of performance metrics, a ChatGPT ad click visit to an advertiser’s website generated about one-third the revenue of a paid search visit in U.S. traffic. The working paper in my Nov. 2 coverage provided the pooled revenue metric from 102 different websites with transaction and revenue tracking. The authors of that paper called the comparison descriptive. One of the authors’ universities also released a press statement saying that for every dollar an advertiser spends on ChatGPT Ads, they receive $0.52 back in revenue (compared to $3.40 for every dollar spent on Google Search).

Only the first of these performance metrics was actually measured. The second figure combined that measured performance metric with the average cost-per-click pricing from one ChatGPT account and the median cost-per-click pricing from 16 paid search accounts. So the second figure varies with what an advertiser pays per click on each of those channels.

An Oct. 21 engineering post from OpenAI puts the run rate above $1 billion, with more than 100,000 advertisers having run ads since launch. Alphabet reported $63.35 billion in Search & other revenue for the third quarter, up 12%, which I covered on Oct. 28.

On Alphabet’s earnings call, Chief Business Officer Philipp Schindler cited “the lower monetization we were seeing in AI Mode” as one factor in slower Search growth, without giving a figure or a baseline.

Google Search was the most-mentioned potential source of future ChatGPT ad spending in a Bank of America survey of 117 advertisers and agencies, TheStreet reported on Oct. 14. I haven’t seen the bank’s note, and the survey asked about plans. It doesn’t measure money that has moved.

Neither company’s revenue figures show spending that shifted from one platform to the other. Google can continue to grow even as some advertisers move part of their budgets elsewhere.

In U.S. traffic, paid search generated $2.45 in revenue per session versus $0.89 with ChatGPT ad sessions, and transactions per session came to 1.17% against 0.37%.

These pooled figures are based on a total of 60 weeks (through Aug. 22). For U.S. traffic, there were up to 28 weeks of ChatGPT ad sessions available for analysis.

Kaiser and Schulze built a statistical model that controlled for website, device type, and week, and found that ChatGPT ad sessions generated lower rates of conversion and lower revenue per session than paid search. These results were robust even after removing individual advertisers. Out of 87 different advertisers who used both paid search and ChatGPT ads in U.S. traffic, 84 produced less revenue per session using ChatGPT ads.

About 20% of the 102 websites studied were services, software, education, or finance websites. A table footnote explains that these websites report online conversions as bookings, leads, licenses, or sign-ups. However, the appendix calls a transaction a completed order, and it does not explain how the authors defined the relationship between these two types of metrics.

Because advertisers chose to buy ChatGPT ads, the authors do not argue causally that ChatGPT is worse for advertisers than paid search. Rather, the authors view their work as “descriptive rather than causal,” a record of what these websites received from each advertising channel. They do not provide any evidence as to whether switching advertising dollars from paid search to ChatGPT under matched campaigns would be beneficial or detrimental to specific advertisers.

Data for this study were donated by Grips Intelligence, where Kaiser, a former employee, works as a scientific advisor. The authors disclose that Kaiser has received a salary and virtual company shares from Grips Intelligence. The authors add that Grips Intelligence played no role in conducting the research described in this study.

I contacted OpenAI about this study and received an email response from an OpenAI spokesperson saying the study “captures an earlier period of ChatGPT Ads’ development and extrapolates platform performance from a small sample.” The statement also says OpenAI has kept launching products since the ads launched, with Target CPA and Target CPC among the recent ones.

Kaiser and Schulze express the difference in terms of value for money, revenue per session divided by click price. Treating each session as a paid click, that works out to about $0.52 per ad dollar for ChatGPT ($0.89 ÷ $1.72) and $3.40 for search ($2.45 ÷ $0.72), the two figures in the Frankfurt School release. The authors report that an ad visit from ChatGPT returns about one-third the value of a search visit at about 2.4 times the price. In their abstract, they state that ChatGPT ads are worth less than a sixth the value for money of Google Search. A table provides a reported ChatGPT price of 6.57 times what would be necessary to produce the same return on investment as Search.

The Frankfurt School release cites the difference as “6.6 times better value for money” for Google and reports this in revenue per ad dollar. Its $0.52 and $3.40 figures are not provided within the body of the paper, and the release itself gives no explanation of how they were calculated.

There is no single price given for search, but rather a median price of $0.72, which comes from 16 mostly U.S. accounts that have linked Google Ads cost records. This price was not matched to the revenue each site generated.

The ChatGPT price is $1.72, which Opascope, an agency that runs paid media for clients, published in June. It covers one account and about $60,000 in spend over 15 days, on campaigns the agency scaled after they showed promise. Opascope wrote that the numbers aren’t an average of every test it launched, and it reported a 1.49x ROAS.

Just one website in the sample did as well as Opascope’s account on both conversion rate and implied revenue per visit, and it had only nine ChatGPT ad sessions.

The authors suggest that $1.72 is a conservative price as it is toward the low end of what practitioners report and below the $3-$5 OpenAI suggests be used as a starting maximum bid. Also, bidding is based on a maximum value, which is simply the cap an advertiser sets, not necessarily what each click will cost.

Resampling advertisers, while keeping the search price constant, gives the authors a range of $0.05 to $0.57 around a ChatGPT click price of about $0.26 that would match search’s return. Neither the ChatGPT click price nor the search price was changed.

Advertising agencies have provided reports about their individual ChatGPT Ads campaign data for one advertiser, and separately, Brooke Osmundson reported in September that advertisers lacked the context to assess what they were being told by the numbers in such reporting.

StubGroup provides ChatGPT ads management services. It ran Google ad campaigns and ChatGPT Ads campaigns for an advertiser who is a B2B compliance company, for 30 days. The clicks on ChatGPT ads cost $0.76 a click. The clicks on Google search campaigns cost $10.46 a click. The cost per lead with ChatGPT was $92.21; with Google it was $157.57. The conversion rates were 0.8% with ChatGPT, and 6.64% with Google.

The agency said that while the advertising campaigns run through Google have years of optimization behind them, the leads generated through those campaigns appear to be converting to customers at a greater rate so far than the leads generated through ChatGPT ads. As a result of this, the cost per customer appears to be lower for Google. How many customers will be ultimately generated from the leads created through both platforms, StubGroup does not yet know, due to the client’s long sales cycle. Additionally, the agency said that the $0.76 per click was low when compared to the CPCs of some of its other clients.

Workshop Digital used its own funds to pay for $2,319 worth of clicks on ChatGPT Ads. Workshop Digital’s CPC for ChatGPT ads was $3.14. For Google Search the CPC was $6.76. The CTR for Workshop Digital’s ChatGPT ads was 1.1%. For Google, the CTR was 5.2%.

Workshop Digital received zero qualified leads from its ChatGPT ads, and two qualified leads from Google. The agency called the two types of advertising campaigns “not a direct comparison,” although it didn’t provide the spend amount or dates for Google Search as part of the comparison.

Brafton, which sells ChatGPT Ads services, ran one click campaign with one ad from June 17 to Aug. 28. It spent $1,524.11 for 263 clicks and one form submission. Its Google and LinkedIn comparisons are outside benchmarks, and its director of paid media, Zach Shah, said ChatGPT ads are “priced like search, but seem to behave like paid social.”

All three agency reports came down to what happened after the click, the stage with the fewest results.

Additionally, OpenAI pointed me to some customer success stories via its ad page. One such example is from Jotform. According to this example, their cost per signup is approximately 30% less than with paid search. This figure is based on Jotform’s internal data collected during July; however, no costs are provided behind it, nor does it detail how the sign-ups were attributed. Sign-ups do not equal sales.

A paid search team may be asked to shift some portion of search spend to ChatGPT on the strength of a per-dollar figure based upon another party’s click costs. For an account paying a number of dollars per click on search, a number greater than the median of the paper’s data, there are differing starting points for making such comparisons. The basis for comparison that makes sense begins with actual spend and attributed revenue on each channel for the same period of time and using the same attribution settings.

The size of the test will affect how much an ecommerce account testing ChatGPT Ads can learn from a weak result. In all, 18 of the paper’s 102 sites recorded transactions resulting from ChatGPT ads; a single zero does not distinguish a weak channel from a small test. So when reporting to stakeholders, the number of sessions associated with each ad campaign belongs beside the revenue figures, because what a zero means is quite different depending on whether there were a few dozen or a few thousand visits.

To compare results, lead-gen accounts also need to define a qualified lead in exactly the same terms on both channels and give those leads sufficient opportunity to convert. This is why StubGroup’s customer comparison is still open, since its lower-cost leads have not yet turned into lower-cost customers. While a cost per signup was used by Jotform as the metric in their case study, it is further removed from revenue than a cost per customer.

A team planning to present Ads Manager results either against the paper’s data or against its Google Ads performance metrics will first need to document its attribution settings. On OpenAI’s Measure Results page, Ads Manager conversion totals may include eligible view-through conversions, and advertisers select from a 7-day, 14-day, or 30-day click window. The view-through window can be set to one day or disabled, and both windows employ last-touch logic. The paper tracked visits that were attributable to the ad.

Ads Manager tracks clicks, while analytics uses sessions. There can be differences between these two numbers. On OpenAI’s basics page, the company says ad-review crawling programs may access landing pages that contain tracking parameters, and analytics tools may report these visits as paid traffic even if they do not represent billable clicks. The Measure Results page provides additional explanations for these discrepancies, including redirects, consent settings, and browser-based blocking. Only by assuming clicks and sessions align can the release’s $0.52 be calculated from reported revenue per session and cost per click.

OpenAI’s ads FAQ says that they do not currently provide performance benchmarks. In addition, all four OpenAI help pages I reviewed provided a suggested starting bid, but none provided any information about click prices across advertisers. Neither did OpenAI’s statement. One advertiser’s cost is documented in the research paper. Each agency CPC was unique to its specific case.

There were no monthly or bid-type breakdowns within the research paper, so it could not establish if the outcomes had been affected by OpenAI adding conversion-optimized campaigns in June. Data from the research paper ceased prior to when OpenAI implemented bid adjustments, which went into effect this month.

On Oct. 28, Google published an ads post stating that CTR for sponsored and organic product listings in AI Mode were similar. This was based on two weeks of internal U.S. data. Google gave no absolute rates. That was the single performance figure for AI Mode ads in my review of Google documentation.

Two of the bid options now offered for new ChatGPT Ads campaigns didn’t exist during the paper’s data window. Since Nov. 9, new conversion campaigns that want a cost target use Target CPA, and new click campaigns can use Target CPC, as I covered this week. The option with no cost target is Intelligent bidding, previously named Maximize Results, according to OpenAI’s bidding page. Beginning with Nov. 18, all values submitted using the legacy API bid fields are treated as the average-cost target when creating a new campaign or changing an ad group’s bid type. Max Bid and Max CPC will officially retire for existing campaigns on Jan. 1, 2027.

Performance improvement is not shown in the new options. Noting which objective, bid strategy, and attribution windows produced each fourth-quarter result will help a team decide if the metrics generated this year have enough similarities to compare next year.

#7422. Customer Growth Manager at Uscreen

Uscreen is the video monetization platform for businesses building recurring revenue from video content. Our customers replace a patchwork stack of separate hosting, community, courses, email, and app vendors with one branded experience across web, mobile, and TV.

The platform is only half of it. We believe growth requires behavior, not just software. Customers don't stall because a feature is missing. They stall because they priced wrong, never built an email list, or launched an offer nobody wanted. Coaching is how we fix that, and it's part of the product rather than an add-on.

You own a segment, and you run it like a growth marketer.

We have a cohort of smaller video businesses where retention is not where it should be. Nobody owns it today. You will. The revenue that stays in that segment, and the revenue that grows inside it, is yours.

This is a coaching role for someone with a growth marketer's mindset. We wouldn't hire a demand gen marketer who couldn't analyze the state of the business and figure out what's needed, and we won't hire a coach who can't either. You'll look at a customer's business the way an owner would: where the revenue comes from, where it leaks, and what to do next. You pull your own numbers to get there. When a customer needs a custom report to answer a growth question, you build it yourself.

It's a one-to-many job. Your cohort is larger than a 1:1 book, so the work is designing coaching that scales: cohort programs, group sessions, office hours, and triggered outreach when the data says a business is drifting. You'll build that motion rather than inherit it.

Success is measured in dollars: gross revenue retention in your cohort first, expansion second. Not tickets closed, not calls booked.

A coach with a growth marketer's mindset. Maybe you've run growth or demand gen for a small business, built your own audience, or coached founders through their numbers. You understand how a membership business makes money, you pull your own analytics to see what's working, and you're comfortable doing it in front of a client. What matters is that you can find the real constraint in a business, then sit with the operator and say the honest thing.

#7420. With event costs up and funding down, journalism organizations cancel conferences and cut staff

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

ONA, OpenNews, and others see troubled times ahead, so it’s goodbye to “rubber chicken dinners.”

RELATED ARTICLEWe know coronavirus has wrecked the events business for media in 2020. But will it come back post-virus?Joshua BentonMarch 25, 2020When the pandemic forced conferences to go virtual, the question was whether people would come back in person post-Covid.

For a while, they did. For a couple years after the pandemic, people were excited to be in person together again. U.S. journalism organizations saw their revenue climb, as sponsors and funders spent generously.

At the end of 2026, though, the situation is less rosy. Combine surging jet fuel prices, inflation, media companies cutting costs, and declining sponsor and funder dollars, and the future appears grim not just for journalism conferences but, in some cases, for the organizations behind them.

Revenue is the total revenue line on each organization’s IRS Form 990. The 990s are from ProPublica’s Nonprofit Explorer. ONA’s 990 for 2025 was not available as of November 12, 2026.

The Online News Association said on Tuesday that it is “pausing” its 26-year-old conference and laying off its five staffers.

“Before the pandemic, the annual conference was ONA’s biggest source of revenue, and together with grants, it sustained the organization. This is no longer true,” Niketa Patel wrote. “The costs of large convenings have climbed sharply while professional development and sponsorship budgets have shrunk.”

LION Publishers said in September that it’s getting out of the large conference business for now. “Philanthropy is famously fickle, and funding priorities have shifted, making this kind of conference a very tough lift,” executive director Chris Krewson added.

LION barely broke even on the conferences it held in 2025 and 2026, Krewson told me. The organization may still hold smaller events next year, it’s not cutting staff or programming, and it’s expanding its Audit program. But it “won’t be taking on the responsibility for an independent event at a hotel with a food and beverage minimum and hotel room block for 400-plus people.”

“Every dollar I spend on rubber chicken dinners and microphones/WiFi for three days is money I can’t spend on programs that make publishers’ businesses stronger,” Krewson said.

OpenNews said in October that it’s switching into “emergency mode”1 and cutting back on “work that distills journalism craft: no more community calls or Source articles for at least the rest of 2026 and maybe longer.”

The future of OpenNews’s annual conference, SRCCON, is uncertain. “We usually make our decision about SRCCON at about this time every year, but this year is different as we consider the news from both LION and ONA and the funding pressures that we know all too well,” Jessica Morrison, co–executive director of OpenNews, told me in an email. “We are opening a community conversation today — emails going out very soon — to gather input about SRCCON, our other programs, and where we go next with OpenNews.”

The three-year-old Organization for Accessible Journalism said Thursday that it is shutting down. “Financial support never reached a level that allowed us to build beyond an all volunteer effort — including my full-time effort,” founder Stacy Kess wrote.

Journalism conferences in the United States are certainly not gone. IRE and NICAR will hold their annual data journalism conference in Denver in March. The Institute for Nonprofit News is “talking about what INN Days will look like in 2027” and will know more by early next year. And the International Symposium on Journalism is on for 2027 — its 28th year, founder (and Nieman Foundation board member) Rosental Alves told me. But things have gotten harder, he said. “It’s not only the difficulty of finding sponsors, but also the rising costs of venues, hotels, airfares, etc., compounded by shrinking travel budgets in newsrooms and even the problems international attendees face in coming to the U.S.,” he told me in an email. ISOJ cut costs, in part by moving to a different venue, and it benefits from being relatively small. “It’s very sad that foundations and corporations that funded journalism conferences in the past have pulled back their support,” Alves added. “The need for these gatherings is as great as ever.” a play on Emergency Mode for News, its initiative to support journalists working during disasters [↩]

On Wednesday, Meta, TikTok, and Google testified in the Indonesian parliament in opposition to a new copyright bill. The proposed law would require digital platforms to pay news publishers in Indonesia for aggregating and previewing their content, according to a new report from Reuters.

RELATED ARTICLEThis citizen-run organization is teaching thousands of Indonesians to fact-checkHanaa' TameezApril 12, 2023The bill does not distinguish between aggregation and republication. Tech platforms would have to pay even when they surface news link previews or story snippets in their products, including AI search products. The law would also force platforms to compensate publishers when their journalism is used to train AI models.

Any compensation would be paid through a state-run management organization, which would then distribute the funds to publishers. Platforms that don’t comply could face sanctions, including the loss of their local business permits.

If the bill does pass, Indonesia would become the first country in Southeast Asia to formally fold AI into its copyright law.

Social media and search engine companies have come out in force against the bill, with Google leading the campaign.

Indonesia is a massive market for global digital platforms with roughly 230 million internet users. In 2023, Indonesia had the fifth-most Google users of any country in the world, with traffic reaching 4.42 billion searches.

RELATED ARTICLEMeta will remove legit news from Facebook and Instagram in Canada — but may leave the bad stuff upLaura Hazard OwenAugust 2, 2023As of October 2026, 92% of internet users in Indonesia reported using WhatsApp, with Instagram and Facebook falling close behind at 84% and 79% respectively, according to We Are Social’s Digital 2027 report.

On Wednesday, a Google official argued that the bill would limit access to news, according to Reuters.

Berni Moestafa, Meta’s head of public policy in Indonesia, testified that if the bill is passed “publishers could lose readership traffic as well as potential advertising and subscription revenue.”

Back in 2023, Canada passed the Online News Act, its own, albeit narrower law which required platforms like Google and Meta to pay publishers for sharing or linking to their content. Meta responded by blocking news links on Facebook and Instagram in Canada altogether.

#7415. When The WordPress Plugin Update Is The Security Risk: Why SEOs Should Pay Attention via @sejournal, @cshel

Webinar: 9 AI Workflows For Better Content. Nov 18, 2 PM ET.

Assess SEO risks from compromised WordPress plugin updates with deployment records and file checks that reveal what version numbers alone cannot.

I’ve worked with WordPress for more than 20 years, and for most of that time, keeping plugins updated has been among the first recommendations I’ve made when discussing website security. It’s still good advice. Known vulnerabilities don’t become less dangerous because updating a site is inconvenient. The advice does carry an assumption that most of us rarely bother to examine: The update we’re installing is the software its developer actually intended to release.

For SEOs, this is more than an abstract concern about application security. When someone gets unauthorized access to a website, they may change the pages search engines see, introduce spam, tamper with redirects or indexing directives, or alter content without the editorial team’s knowledge. We can spend days investigating those symptoms as routine technical SEO problems while completely missing the reason they’re happening.

There have now been several recent WordPress incidents in which the trusted delivery mechanism was part of the problem, so let’s look at them together. Examining them as a group is more illuminating than treating any single developer’s bad week as the big story.

In June 2024, malicious updates appeared in several WordPress.org-hosted plugins, including Social Warfare. Wordfence’s investigation traced the compromise to developer accounts that used previously exposed credentials. The injected code could create administrator accounts and exfiltrate information, and researchers also found code designed to inject SEO spam. Roughly 35,000 installations were potentially exposed, although Wordfence couldn’t say how many had actually received the malicious updates. This is an especially useful example for our profession because the search-related damage wasn’t hypothetical: SEO spam was part of the attacker’s toolkit.

The following July, Gravity Forms disclosed that some copies of versions 2.9.11.1 and 2.9.12 available for manual download had been modified maliciously. According to Gravity Forms’ incident notice, the exposure was confined to particular manual downloads and Composer installations during July 9-10, 2025. Its separate automatic-update service was not compromised. That distinction is important. Two organizations could have been using ostensibly the same software while facing different risks because they obtained it through different channels.

The more recent incident involved Rank Math SEO PRO. Rank Math’s incident disclosure says a subset of version 3.0.123 packages downloaded or updated from October 15 at 20:02 UTC through October 16 at 07:12 UTC contained malware capable of compromising sites if activated. Rank Math removed the affected files, provided a clean 3.0.124 release, and advised affected customers to treat their installations as compromised. Wordfence’s advisory classified the issue as critical, with a CVSS score of 9.8. The free Rank Math plugin distributed through WordPress.org was not affected.

The three cases aren’t identical. One involved compromised developer accounts and poisoned repository updates, another concerned certain official manual downloads, and the third affected specific packages of a commercial SEO plugin. They do, however, share a problem that ordinary update advice doesn’t adequately address: the site owner could get into trouble while obtaining software from a source they had good reason to trust.

The Rank Math release timeline makes this unusually clear. According to the Rank Math changelog, version 3.0.123 appeared on Oct. 7, but the affected distribution window didn’t begin until Oct. 15. A site reporting that version number might have received the original clean files or a compromised package, depending on when it was updated. The installed version alone cannot resolve the question.

Imagine managing a hundred client sites, or an enterprise portfolio with different brands, teams, and hosting providers. A security advisory comes out and somebody asks which properties are exposed. You can generate a tidy plugin inventory in minutes, but a spreadsheet of version numbers may not tell you what was actually installed. You need deployment timestamps, a record of the package source and, where possible, a way to compare the installed files with verified clean artifacts. Gravity Forms presented a related challenge because the installation method determined whether a particular download was implicated.

I don’t expect SEO practitioners to start auditing build pipelines. I do expect us to understand the limits of the information we routinely use to assess the health of a site. A dashboard that says a plugin is current doesn’t certify that the underlying files are trustworthy, and installing a clean update doesn’t necessarily remove accounts, backdoors, or stolen credentials left behind during a compromise.

See also: From Plugins To Performance: What CMOs Need To Ask About Their WordPress Stack

In an enterprise environment, ownership of the website is often split across several groups. Marketing may choose the SEO software, development handles deployments, a hosting provider manages updates, and security gets called when someone notices suspicious activity. The SEO team is nevertheless expected to account for what the search engines can crawl, index, and understand. Those responsibilities overlap whether the organizational chart acknowledges it or not.

Consider how a compromise might first appear in our regular work. Search Console begins reporting unfamiliar URLs. A crawl finds redirects that weren’t present last week. Canonical tags have changed without a corresponding release, or the rendered page no longer matches what the content team published. Depending on the attacker’s access, visitors, and crawlers might even be served different content. None of those observations proves a security breach, and I am not suggesting they were documented outcomes of the Rank Math incident. They are reasons to include compromise in the set of explanations we consider instead of assuming every unexpected technical change is a configuration error.

That can be particularly consequential when an SEO has spotted a symptom but doesn’t know whom to tell. We don’t need to become the malware response team. We do need an established route for escalating suspicious changes, preferably one worked out before an incident has everyone comparing logs and asking who owns what. The 2024 SEO-spam injection case demonstrates why that coordination belongs in an SEO conversation rather than being filed away as somebody else’s security problem.

See also: Who Owns Web Performance? Building A Framework For Digital Accountability

WordPress itself has been looking at the trust problem. In June 2026, Matt Mullenweg announced Protect the Shire, initially describing a cooldown for new plugin and theme releases before they reached sites through WordPress.org’s automatic-update infrastructure. WordPress has also documented an automated security review process intended to identify potentially risky changes. The appeal is straightforward: a period of scrutiny may catch a compromised release before it is distributed widely, although delaying a genuine emergency fix creates a competing risk.

That protection has boundaries. Commercial plugins delivered by their vendors’ own update systems don’t necessarily pass through the same WordPress.org review process, even though all the plugins appear in the same administrative interface. The FAIR project, operating under Linux Foundation governance, is taking a different approach by developing federated and independent software repositories. Protect the Shire focuses on checks within one major distribution route, while FAIR focuses on diversifying and verifying the routes themselves. Neither approach should be mistaken for a guarantee that every package reaching a website is safe.

For people responsible for websites, the practical question is less about choosing a philosophical side in the distribution debate and more about knowing where each update originates and what checks apply along the way.

An SEO team doesn’t need to turn every plugin upgrade into a full security review. It would be useful, though, to know whether the organization retains update dates and deployment records, whether its commercial plugins use separate delivery systems, and who can verify file integrity when a vendor identifies an affected download window. It is equally worth knowing whether the recovery plan extends beyond restoring yesterday’s backup to checking for unauthorized accounts, persistence mechanisms, and exposed credentials.

I would also ask who receives reports of suspicious URLs, unexpected redirects, or changes to indexing instructions. We already know how to inspect rendered pages, compare crawls, review logs, and investigate search performance anomalies. Those skills make us quite capable of noticing that a website isn’t behaving as it should. They don’t automatically tell us why, which is where an agreed escalation process becomes useful.

None of this is a reason to stop updating plugins, or an excuse to infer that a particular vendor is incompetent because it experienced an incident. The root cause of a compromise cannot responsibly be guessed from the fact that malware turned up in a package. What these examples do show is that familiar update channels and reassuring version numbers aren’t the whole story. We spend a great deal of time checking what a website actually serves rather than trusting what a configuration screen says it should serve. It seems reasonable to apply some of that same curiosity to the software we’re installing on it.

Featured Image: LookerStudio/Shutterstock

From new majors to search traffic, newspapers to impeachment: Have you kept up with this week’s media news?

It’s been another busy week. Recap it with the second edition of the Nieman Lab News-About-News Quiz, your weekly incentive to keep up with the latest happenings in the world of digital journalism. All questions are based on the week’s Nieman Lab stories or articles elsewhere that we’ve linked to in What We’re Reading. The quiz will appear here through November as a trial run; if people seem to like it, we’ll keep it going in 2027. Good luck!

What journalism organization announced this week that it was canceling its annual conference and laying off most of its staff?

“Since we gathered in Chicago for ONA26, many of you have asked when we will be together again,” CEO Niketa Patel wrote. “Unfortunately, it will not be in 2027. ONA has decided to pause our in-person events and will not host a conference in 2027.”

For the first time ever, the press freedom group Reporters Without Borders (RSF) has officially called for the impeachment of a U.S. official. Which one?

“RSF does not take the question of impeachment lightly. In fact, our organization has never before called for the removal of a US official. But the severity and persistence of Carr’s misconduct as FCC chairman demand an extraordinary response. Congress has a constitutional responsibility to hold him accountable. Restoring the FCC’s independence must be central to that effort.”

Emerson College recently announced a new degree program aimed at helping students build “a career across a rapidly changing media landscape.” What’s the program’s name?

“Our new Content Creation major prepares students to be a part of the evolving creator economy, teaching them not only how to produce compelling digital content but also how to build a successful entrepreneurial career.”

What news organization — after a challenging few years — says it is now “within striking distance of break-even,” financially?

“I’ll be honest,” executive editor Matt Murphy said at a conference. “We had years of losses, and steepening losses. That’s the truth. We’re a private company and don’t share the figures, but it was hundreds and hundreds of millions of dollars. Now we’re within striking distance of break-even, and I expect next year will be our best year in seven years. We’ve done the right-sizing we needed, which was tough.”

The Echo-Pioneer — the local newspaper in the town of High Level, Alberta (population 4,000) — has an unusual business model. What is it?

Town officials signed a two-year “advertising and readership agreement” in 2025. It’s one of the many ways local Canadian news outlets are trying to stay afloat — most notably the federal Local Journalism Initiative.

Which online publisher’s CEO announced that Google search traffic had “dropped by more than 1 million referrals on average per week” in October?

As a result of the search decline, CEO Steve Huffman announced Reddit would be shifting to a primarily “logged-in experience.”

The Asia-Pacific outlet The Diplomat retracted an interview with a South Korean CEO last week. Why?

“The author presented themselves as a South Korean freelance journalist and claimed to have interviewed Newtype’s CEO. We now know that the journalist fabricated the interview and may not even be who they claimed to be.”

The parliament of an Asian nation is debating requiring tech companies like Google and Meta to pay news outlets when they direct users to their stories. Which nation?

The proposed law would also require compensating news publishers when AI models are trained on news content.

Which international news outlet, sensing a political opening, is expanding its reporting team in the United States?

“Market research indicated there was room to grow among politically liberal Jews in the United States. Gali Arnon, who became the chief executive of Haaretz Group last year, said she wanted the newspaper to become in other countries what it is in Israel: an ‘identity brand.’”

This photo shows an early editorial plan from one of the first important publications on the World Wide Web, a mononymic website that has recently been in the news. What site was it?

The photo is from Salon co-founder Laura Miller, laying out some early “issues” of the influential web “magazine” which closed last week. “People sometimes tell me about reading Salon avidly in their youth, how it felt like connecting to something exhilarating and cool and a bit crazy in the strange new expanses of the internet. All I can say is: That’s exactly how it felt to work there.”

#7412. Partner Solutions Architect , AI Builder at Supabase

Supabase is the Postgres development platform, built by developers for developers. We provide a complete backend solution including Database, Auth, Storage, Edge Functions, Realtime, and Vector Search. All services are deeply integrated and designed for growth.

Supabase is the backend of choice for a growing wave of AI-native builders, and we're deepening structured partnerships with the platforms they build on top of — Anthropic, OpenAI, Vercel, and Lovable. These partners' teams are talking to thousands of developers and agents who need exactly what we build—a full backend platform with Postgres at the core—without the vendor lock-in. This is an opportunity to get Supabase in front of the right partner SAs and make us the default recommendation for a modern, AI-ready backend.

We’re looking for a Platform Solutions Architect to join our Success Team and help embed Supabase into the Solutions and Engineering communities with AI Builders.

You’ll work closely with Partner Solutions Architects and Partner Engineers at Anthropic, OpenAI, Vercel, and Lovable, helping us proactively identify builder problems where Supabase is the right solution and closing the gap between partner intent and real developer outcomes. This role is ideal for someone who thrives in async, fast-paced environments and is excited about building developer tools that scale to millions of AI-native apps and agents.

In this role, you’ll focus on three core pillars:

Build deep relationships with Technical counterparts at Anthropic, OpenAI, Vercel, and Lovable, focusing initially on defined use cases and agent/app-migration motions.

Develop and deliver technical workshops, training materials, and enablement content to give partner SAs the fluency to position Supabase.

Create demos, integration guides, and reference architectures that make Supabase’s fit with Anthropic, OpenAI, Vercel, and Lovable immediately legible.

Partner with SAs at these companies on active opportunities to move deals forward and feeding technical pipeline intelligence back to the alliance lead.

Resolve blockers for partner SAs working on Supabase implementations to maintain their credibility with the builders they support.

Troubleshoot complex integration scenarios and turn solutions into reusable assets.

Maintain a close feedback loop with Supabase product and engineering teams to ensure technical guidance reflects the latest platform capabilities.

Measure success through co-sell opportunities sourced, influenced deals, and SA enablement metrics across the Anthropic, OpenAI, Vercel, and Lovable partnerships.

Write technical blog posts and case studies that demonstrate real-world Supabase implementations built on Anthropic, OpenAI, Vercel, and Lovable.

Represent Supabase at conferences, meetups, and partner-sponsored events (e.g. Anthropic and OpenAI dev days, Vercel Ship, Lovable community events).

Develop video content and interactive learning experiences to reduce the "time-to-fluency" for partner SAs.

Have 5+ years of experience in technical roles with deep hands-on experience building on modern AI infrastructure. Previous experience working at Anthropic, OpenAI, Vercel, Lovable (or a similar AI builder platform) or as a partner to one is required.

Understand how partner SAs at AI builder platforms are incentivized, how they make recommendations, and how the partner ecosystem influences developer decisions.

Communicate clearly across both technical and non-technical audiences, explaining complex concepts with ease.

Have a strong technical foundation in PostgreSQL, APIs, and modern development frameworks like React and Next.js, plus fluency with AI/agent tooling (LLM APIs, MCP, agent frameworks).

Are comfortable navigating ambiguity and moving quickly to build a playbook from scratch.

Are energized by solving real-world problems for developers building the next generation of AI-native products.

We hire globally. We believe you can do your best work from anywhere. There are no Supabase offices, but we provide a WeWork membership or co-working allowance you can use anywhere in the world.

Every team member receives ESOP (equity ownership) in the company. We want everyone to share in the upside of what we’re building together.

Use this budget to set up your ideal work environment—laptop, monitor, headphones, or whatever helps you do your best work.

Supabase covers 100% of health insurance for employees and 80% for dependents, wherever you are. Your wellbeing and your family’s health are important to us.

Once a year, the entire company gathers in a new city for a week of connection, collaboration, and fun. It’s a highlight of our year.

We operate asynchronously and trust you to manage your own time. You know what needs to be done and when.

Every team member receives an annual education allowance to spend on learning—courses, books, conferences, or anything that supports your growth.

Supabase was born-remote and open-source-first. We believe our globally distributed team is our secret weapon in building tools developers love.

Over $1B raised (including our $500M Series F)

We move fast, build in public, and use what we ship. If it’s in your project, we probably use it in ours too. We believe deeply in the open-source ecosystem and strive to support—not replace—existing tools and communities.

New remote jobs delivered to your inbox, every week.

Location independence is the future of work. It serves companies with best talent from around the globe. And benefits employees with a greater work life balance and the ability to work in their pyjamas.- Nithur, founder.

See November 2026 CMS market share and website usage data from W3Techs, including WordPress, Shopify, Wix, and Squarespace, plus the latest platform trends.

WordPress might remain the dominant force in content management systems (CMS) for now, but market share has dropped since its peak in 2022 to under 60%. According to W3Techs on Nov. 13, 2026, WordPress now has a CMS market share of 57.9%. Looking at historical data, WordPress dipped under 60% in 2016, 2017, and 2019, but this is the lowest drop since 2013.

WordPress still remains a substantial lead over its nearest rival, Shopify, but is this an indication of a downturn for WordPress, or for the general usage of CMS?

Shopify has continued its growth across all surveyed websites, with Wix and Squarespace also maintaining their growth trajectory. In fact, apart from Joomla and Drupal, which fell, and Webflow, which held flat, all other top CMS have increased market share, indicating WordPress is on a downturn to the benefit of other platforms.

This report breaks down the current CMS landscape, compares the top platforms, and outlines the latest shifts in market share and usage.

According to W3Techs, 67.7% of websites have a CMS, and Netcraft reports over 323 million domains

From this, we can assume that the current market size for content management systems has risen to 218.8 million websites.

*Approximations extrapolated from W3Techs and Netcraft data

There are two different measures throughout this report: usage is a platform’s percentage of all surveyed websites, while market share is its percentage of websites with a known CMS.

Data from W3Techs, Nov. 13, 2026. (WooCommerce and Elementor are not listed in the table above as they’re WordPress plugins and not standalone CMS platforms.)

*Graphs are separated due to the dominance of the WordPress market share.

WordPress remains the most widely used CMS. Its usage across all surveyed websites rose from 23.3% in January 2015 to 43.2% in January 2022, before falling to 39.2% today.

But its long-standing growth curve is now in a downturn. Its CMS market share has fallen by approximately 7.3 percentage points from the January 2022 figure of 65.2%. Since Jan. 1, 2026, it has declined from 60.2% to 57.9%, while all-website usage has dropped from 43.0% to 39.2%.

Those figures do not show why individual sites changed platforms. For teams using WordPress, plugin compatibility, core updates, and security management remain practical considerations.

Read more: Should You Still Use WordPress?

As the second-most popular standalone CMS in W3Techs’ current listing, Shopify’s market share stands at 7.9%, and it is used by 5.4% of all websites surveyed. Both measures have increased from Jan. 1, 2026, when they stood at 7.0% and 5.0%, respectively.

Market share is not a performance benchmark. For a separate, historical comparison of technical performance, see our 2025 Core Web Vitals CMS rankings.

From an SEO and business perspective, Shopify’s growing footprint makes it a platform worth evaluating alongside the features, costs, and technical requirements of an online store.

Wix now powers 4.2% of websites surveyed and holds 6.2% of the known-CMS market. Its market share has increased from 5.8% at the start of 2026, but its all-website usage remains at 4.2% at the displayed precision.

Wix has benefited from its positioning beyond a lightweight website builder that consistently invests in branding and platform capabilities, making it a viable contender for mid-market adoption.

Squarespace’s CMS market share has grown from 0.5% in January 2015 to 3.6% today, with 2.4% of all websites surveyed now using the platform.

Its growth could be attributed to the increasing demand for low-maintenance, design-forward platforms that are easily accessible to small businesses and individuals.

Read more: WordPress Vs. Squarespace – Which One Is Better?

In contrast to all the other top CMS surveyed, Joomla and Drupal have continued to lose CMS market share, now accounting for 1.6% and 0.9%, respectively. At the start of 2026, those figures were 1.9% and 1.1%.

Once platforms in favor with web developers and amateur coders, this shift likely reflects a broader trend where more user-friendly, SaaS-based platforms capture the attention of small businesses and non-technical users.

Webflow, which last year looked like a growing contender, now holds at 1.2% of the known-CMS market, unchanged from Jan. 1, 2026. Its usage across all surveyed websites has slipped from 0.9% to 0.8%.

Between Jan. 1 and Nov. 13, 2026, the proportion of websites using none of W3Techs’ monitored CMS platforms rose from 28.6% to 32.3%, an increase of approximately 3.7 percentage points. During the same period, WordPress usage fell from 43.0% to 39.2% of all surveyed websites.

That reverses the earlier downward trend in the “no CMS” category. It is not proof that those sites are custom-coded or have abandoned a CMS, as the category means that no monitored CMS was detected.

Since January 2024, Joomla’s CMS market share has fallen from 2.5% to 1.6%, while Drupal’s has declined from 1.6% to 0.9%. Over the longer period, Joomla has dropped from 8.6% in January 2015 and Drupal from 5.1% in the same month.

They’ve slipped from the No. 2 and No. 3 spots to No. 5 and No. 10, overtaken by faster-growing platforms like Wix and Squarespace in 2022.

Joomla, in particular, had strong momentum early on – briefly surpassed WordPress in search interest until around 2008, according to Google Trends – but it hasn’t kept pace with modern platform demands.

Shopify is the platform with the most interest overtaking WordPress.

Why did these popular content management systems decline so much?

It’s most likely due to the strength of third-party support for WordPress with plugins and themes, making it much more accessible. But the rise of supported themes and plugins for Shopify is starting to gain on WordPress.

The growth of website builders, such as Wix and Squarespace, indicates that small businesses want a more straightforward managed solution, and they have started to nibble on market share from the bottom. Although, it does not establish that users moved directly from Joomla or Drupal to those platforms.

Over the period from November 2025 to November 2026, the CMS market share of:

Growth has slowed sharply for Wix and Squarespace, while Shopify’s has accelerated from 4.6% to 16.2% and taken the lead against the others in a reversal from the last reported period (Wix was growing by 32.6%, Squarespace 9.7%, and Shopify by 4.6%).

As mentioned above, SaaS web builders don’t require coding knowledge and offer an opportunity for a small business to get a web presence quickly. The rise of Shopify could be attributed to an influx to the platform from WooCommerce, as the WordPress alternative.

WordPress is not known as a complicated platform to use, but it does require some coding knowledge and an understanding of how websites are built. On the other hand, a website builder is a much easier route to market, without the need to understand what is happening in the back end.

Elementor is the most widely used WordPress page builder, installed on 18.2% of all websites with a known CMS and 12.3% of all sites surveyed (not shown below) – more than Wix and Squarespace combined – though it functions as a plugin within WordPress, not a standalone CMS.

While not a CMS on its own, it is a major part of the WordPress ecosystem. Its figures overlap with WordPress and should not be added to WordPress’s market share or usage.

W3Techs also compares platforms by overall popularity and traffic rank. The ranking bars measure a platform’s share among sites with a known CMS within each ranking tier, rather than its share of all websites.

The WordPress, Joomla, and Drupal comparison above shows Drupal with a smaller overall footprint but a stronger presence among highly ranked sites. WordPress remains much more widely used overall.

Wix and Squarespace have lower representation in the top-ranked groups than in the overall known-CMS sample. That is a traffic-ranking distinction, not a direct measure of business size or the quality of the software.

Elementor gives site owners a visual way to build within WordPress. For businesses comparing drag-and-drop tools, the practical question remains how the builder fits their design, maintenance, and SEO requirements.

WooCommerce has seen a decline to 11.4% of websites with a known CMS, while Shopify has increased to 7.9%.

WooCommerce powers 7.7% of all websites surveyed, compared with Shopify’s 5.4%. As a WordPress-based ecommerce platform, it is included within the WordPress ecosystem rather than listed as a separate standalone CMS in the top 10 above.

W3Techs’ separate ecommerce-system survey uses a different denominator: websites using an ecommerce system that W3Techs monitors. On that measure, WooCommerce has a 47.0% share and Shopify 32.7%. Those figures do not measure sales, revenue, or every online store worldwide.

In comparison to other ecommerce CMS platforms, WooCommerce is still dominant right now.

It has more market share than its competitors combined: Shopify (7.9%) + PrestaShop (0.7%) + OpenCart (0.4%). But it is losing ground, and this could be correlated to the decline of WordPress and users moving to other platforms. It will be interesting to see if Shopify overtakes in the next year.

The ranking comparison also shows why overall adoption is only part of the picture. Shopify has a stronger presence than WooCommerce in several of the higher-ranked groups, even though WooCommerce has the larger overall share of the known-CMS sample.

Shopify surged during the pandemic, with market share growing by 52.9% from 2020 to 2021 and then 26.9% from 2021 to 2022, outpacing every other platform. After a dip in 2023, it recovered in 2024 and has reached 7.9% market share this year.

As the market changes, platform choice affects site architecture, plugin availability, and technical SEO flexibility.

WordPress continues to lead, but its gradual decline marks a turning point. SaaS competitors such as Shopify, Wix, and Squarespace are steadily gaining traction, offering streamlined platforms that appeal to most businesses.

If more SMBs are switching to website builders, understanding the limitations and intricacies of these platforms for SEO could be a competitive advantage. CMS adoption determines how efficiently teams can build, secure, and optimize sites at scale.

The one area I am most interested in is how AI and vibecoding might impact CMS platforms and if there will be a rise in websites without a CMS.

Shopify now runs on 5.4% of all websites surveyed, not just sites with a CMS. With its increasing footprint, specializing in Shopify SEO could be a strategic move for an SEO professional.

Wix and Squarespace remain important alternatives, too. Getting fluent in their ecosystems could help you serve businesses with different development and maintenance requirements.

The reality is that WordPress remains the largest ecosystem in this survey, while other platforms give business leaders and SEO professionals an opportunity to diversify their expertise.

Understanding the strengths and limitations of various CMS platforms can inform strategic decisions and align with evolving market demands.

CMS usage and market-share data collected from W3Techs on Nov. 13, 2026. Historical comparisons use the dates stated in the text. Percentages are rounded by the source, so calculated changes are approximate. See the W3Techs methodology page for how the survey is compiled. Google Trends measures search interest separately.

#7409. Patchstack: Senior Product Manager

Patchstack protects WordPress sites for hosts, agencies and developers, and we're now launching a security product for people building JavaScript apps with AI tools like Claude Code. That product is early. We have good signals from hosts and hackathons, but we haven't yet found who it serves best, what they value, or why they'll keep paying for it.

You'll be the product manager who finds that out. You'll talk to customers, use the product in real AI-assisted workflows, test ideas quickly with our designer and engineers, and build the measurement that tells us what's working. You'll work alongside two small engineering squads, a senior product designer, QA and infrastructure. You own which customer problems we invest in and how we learn from the results.

You're happiest early, before the answers exist. You'd rather run a small test this week than wait for perfect data. You're comfortable in a terminal and have built things with AI-assisted tools, so you can use our product the way our customers do. You form your own view on technical claims rather than taking "it's not feasible" or "the metric improved" at face value. You say what you think, including when it's awkward, and you change your mind when the evidence says so. You work well in a flat team with little process, and you help people around you get better rather than taking work off them.

This is a fully remote job, based anywhere in Europe.

No forms. Just smart, optimized applications.

Remember every detail and next step, without a meeting bot.

#7408. Traffic is declining for local newspapers. Here are some things that helped small publishers make gains.

The Cornell Daily Sun saw traffic spike by almost 500% in September.

RELATED ARTICLESearch traffic has declined so much that some publishers are considering opting out of Google entirelyNeel DhaneshaJuly 22, 2026We’ve now been publishing roundups of local newspaper traffic for a full year, so we can compare this year’s traffic to last year’s. Almost across the board, local newspapers are seeing traffic decline as Google referrals drop. For July, August, and September, traffic to the most-visited sites is lower than at this time last year, according to our Similarweb data.

RELATED ARTICLEHow did newspapers in places like Harrisburg, Birmingham, and Syracuse become some of America’s most-read online?Joshua BentonJuly 23, 2025A good example is Advance Local’s Harrisburg Patriot-News, PennLive.com. Josh has written about Advance publications punching above their weight in traffic. They still are: Advance outlets like AL.com, Mlive.com, and NJ.com, among others, continued to feature prominently in the top sites by estimated monthly visits in July, August, and September. In August 2026, PennLive’s traffic growth stood out even among Advance peers; it gained 3.6 million visits in August compared to July, a 78% spike. But in total, PennLive saw a little over 8.2 million monthly visits for August 2026 — down from about 12.5 million in August 2025.

Still, publishers large and small are finding ways to bring more readers to their sites. In August, the Bozeman Daily Chronicle grew its traffic by about 96,000 monthly visits, a 49% jump. Managing editor Jack Reaney attributed the growth to the newspaper launching a new website Aug. 3 designed for improved functionality, with “fewer, more intentional news categories,” lighter page design for faster load times, and a more modern layout. The Chronicle is one of more than 150 newspapers owned by Adams MultiMedia. The parent company is rolling out the new website design across its newspapers, but Bozeman was the “guinea pig,” Reaney said.

In Florida, Cape Coral Breeze, a small weekly, saw its traffic spike about 139% in August. The network of local weeklies has tried to adopt a daily, real-time mindset after decades of posting once a week, Breeze Newspapers publisher Ray Eckenrode told me. The August spike was driven by participation in Cape Coral Breeze’s “Best of Cape Coral” contest, where readers vote on favorite local businesses in more than 200 categories. According to the team’s internal count, a little over 150,000 “Best of” votes were cast this year, up from 92,000 last year. The team made an effort this year to “drive traffic to our homepage first to reach the contest voting page to expose some of those casual website users to our news coverage,” Eckenrode said, and had some success with that strategy.

In September, The Cornell Daily Sun gained 1 million visits, almost a 500% jump from August, when it broke the story of the Cornell 7 lawsuit (and published an editorial naming the defendants). Other local news sites in New York also saw meaningful growth in September; traffic to NNY360.com jumped 84%, while the Gannett-owned Democrat and Chronicle gained about 762,000 visits, a 35% jump.

On the opposite coast, the San-Jose-based Mercury News gained around 690,000 monthly visits in September, a 14% jump. “Our traffic is volatile like everyone else’s, but we had a strong September mainly because a couple of stories performed very well,” said Annika Toernqvist, MediaNews Group’s managing editor for digital for Northern California. Environmental beat reporter Paul Rogers‘ story about a new California law that will ban watering artificial turf “performed exceptionally well on Google and Google Discovery”; 62% of traffic to the story came from search. Stories about the local impact of new state laws consistently do well with the outlet’s readers, according to Toernqvist, and this was “a hot topic with a strong headline.” The story was also the top subscription converter in September. Another story by Rogers covering the proposed renaming of Fremont State Park also drove traffic that month; 86% came from search, mostly from Google Discovery.

Meanwhile, celebrity reporter Martha Ross‘ story about a new book on King Charles’ valet performed well in part thanks to a bump from…the Drudge Report. (“Yes, the Drudge Report still drives traffic,” Toernqvist said; it accounted for 43% of visits to that story.)

#7407. Senior iOS Engineer, Places at Raya

We are seeking a Senior iOS Engineer to join the Places Client team to build and elevate member-facing experiences across the Places iOS app. The Places Client team is responsible for all surface areas of the mobile app - from onboarding and payments to new initiatives and core features - ensuring our members enjoy a seamless, high-quality iOS experience.

This is a senior client engineering role with deep technical impact across our mobile application. The ideal candidate has built and operated high-scale consumer iOS applications end to end, showing strong ownership from architecture to production execution. You will collaborate closely with product, design, and backend engineering teams to deliver robust features, maintain software health, and drive technical excellence across the codebase.

We are seeking a Senior iOS Engineer to join the Places Client team to build and elevate member-facing experiences across the Places iOS app. The Places Client team is responsible for all surface areas of the mobile app - from onboarding and payments to new initiatives and core features - ensuring our members enjoy a seamless, high-quality iOS experience.

This is a senior client engineering role with deep technical impact across our mobile application. The ideal candidate has built and operated high-scale consumer iOS applications end to end, showing strong ownership from architecture to production execution. You will collaborate closely with product, design, and backend engineering teams to deliver robust features, maintain software health, and drive technical excellence across the codebase.

Build and own core member-facing features end to end.

Set architectural patterns and best practices, and solve hard client-side lifecycle and state management problems.

Partner with server engineering on API design, data correctness, and client-server state sync.

Work with product, design, and data science to scope, experiment with, and launch member-facing features. Sweat the details of interaction, motion, and performance.

Contribute across a large, long-lived iOS codebase: performance, testing practices, and deliberate management of tech debt.

Own production health for core flows: monitoring, crash triage, and release quality.

Raise the engineering bar through code review, mentorship, and clear written specs.

7+ years of professional iOS development experience, with strong proficiency in Swift, UIKit, and MVVM.

Strong experience with RxSwift or similar reactive programming frameworks.

A track record of shipping consumer mobile apps to large audiences, with strong judgment on architecture, performance, and user experience.

Strong consumer product sense, a high bar for design quality, and the ability to partner with product, design, and data.

Proven ability to lead projects from concept through launch, balance speed and quality, and own what you ship after it ships.

You use AI coding tools in your daily work, help the team adopt them, and look for opportunities to improve the engineering harness.

#7406. NPR makes fixing its app a key priority in its new strategic plan

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

Over the next two years, NPR will address a longstanding listener plea: improving its app.

During a November 12 board of directors meeting, NPR CEO Katherine Maher said the organization will rebuild its digital offerings to be a “service-first, app-first destination” as part of NPR’s 2027-2029 strategic plan, Current reported on Thursday. One goal of the plan is to reach “five million weekly active users on its platforms by 2029” and “to build a monthly engaged digital audience of 40 million.” According to Current, Maher said that the NPR network — which includes more than 200 member radio stations — currently reaches 39 million weekly listeners across broadcast and digital, but the “total potential addressable audience, weekly consumers of news, information and culture who are open to our work, is roughly 153 million Americans. That is nearly four times our current reach.”

In Apple’s App Store, NPR’s app has a 4.7-star rating and more than 78,000 reviews, of which the majority are positive. But reviewers have quibbles.

Bryan Moffett, NPR’s senior vice president of transformation, said NPR+, the broadcaster’s subscription program, brought in $8 million in the 2026 fiscal year, up from $5.5 million in 2025. (NPR+ is available with a donation of $8 a month or more, and offers perks like podcasts without ads.) Maher said new investment in the app will help reach younger audiences and shift NPR’s “median audience age from 60-plus toward 40-plus.”

“We love radio, but we have been so wildly successful there that we’ve largely exhausted its further financial growth,” Maher told the board. “And as it shrinks, we must invert our revenue engine to ensure sustainability across all of our platforms, including radio, but to build a wider funnel through digital offerings, third-party platforms, and new investments in marketing and communication that will tell our story and share our value with the world.”

RELATED ARTICLENPR, the quintessential audio news brand, adapts to a video-first futureSarah ScireSeptember 29, 2026Overhauling the app is just one part of NPR’s strategy to keep up with users’ changing consumption preferences. In September, Sarah Scire reported on the broadcaster leaning into video podcasts with the acquisition of Kevin Roose and Casey Newton’s technology podcast Machine Gods. NPR chief operating officer Ryan Merkley told Current in June that NPR was already working on redesigning the app to better serve member stations and their listeners.

“Fix the app,” departing public editor Kelly McBride told NPR leaders during the meeting. “It’s not a great experience for the audience and it’s key to moving forward, but you guys seem like you’re on it. So I won’t dwell on that.”

Nieman Lab requested a copy of the approved strategic plan but did not receive it by publication time. Read the full story in Current here.

#7405. Meta begins internal tests of prediction markets app

Let Social Media Today's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The app would offer similar functionality to Kalshi and Polymarket without involving cash transactions, per the Wall Street Journal.

Meta is seemingly pushing ahead with a controversial plan to introduce a prediction markets element on its platforms. The move comes amid an ongoing debate about the potential harm caused by its apps.

As reported by the Wall Street Journal on Friday, Meta has begun internal testing of its own prediction market app.

As per WSJ: “Employees have begun testing a prediction-market app under development, according to people familiar with the matter, a step the company often takes ahead of a public release.”

WSJ reported that the app, called “Takes,” allows users to wager on the outcome of questions or events. The system does not enable users to place cash bets, but instead uses a system called “cred” that lets users boost their standing in the app by making accurate bets.

Meta has reportedly been developing its own prediction markets tool for the past few months, with the New York Times reporting in June that the company was considering a push into this sector.

Prediction markets have become big business of late, with platforms including Polymarket and Kalshi enabling users to place bets on all sorts of events.

According to the June NYT report, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg had “dispatched a small team at his company to create a smartphone app similar to Polymarket and Kalshi.” NYT said the app would use “a video-game-like points system” instead of letting users bet real money, with Meta hoping to tap into the compulsion of live event betting while avoiding any regulatory scrutiny that would come with financial stakes.

The plan would be for Meta to launch its separate prediction markets app by leveraging Facebook and Instagram for promotion. As such, this wouldn’t be introducing actual gambling into its core apps, but could still provide another way for Meta to benefit from gambling in order to boost engagement.

Which, no matter how Meta frames it, seems like a risky bet.

The company is already facing regulatory scrutiny and legal action around the world due to the harms that its apps have allegedly caused, in particular to younger users.

Younger users are also increasingly likely to engage with prediction markets.

As reported by Reuters: “Just over 60% of users on prediction markets Kalshi and Polymarket are under the age of 35, according to a recent S&P Global Market Intelligence Kagan survey, with sports being the most popular category.”

It would be risky for Meta to go anywhere near this, even without actual money being involved. But, for whatever reason, it seems that Meta is going to try, which could be another example of how the company prioritizes business benefit over user well-being.

Even without involving cash, introducing a betting-like option could be habit-forming, and could inspire people to up their stakes in other apps.

Ask Maps is starting to find appointments online and call local businesses for customers. Here's what Business Profile says about Google's automated calls.

Open appointment slots at beauty, pet care, auto and home-repair businesses are starting to show up in Ask Maps, Google Maps’ AI chat. Google says Ask Maps can look for these appointments online and phone the businesses for a customer.

The feature is part of a set of Ask Maps updates that started rolling out Monday on Android and iOS. Appointment finding is launching first in the U.S.

Business Profile already has a setting for calls Google makes on behalf of customers. Google’s post doesn’t say whether Ask Maps calls follow it.

Google’s post describes appointment finding in Ask Maps this way:

“Now, with new agentic capabilities, you can choose to have Ask Maps find beauty, pet care, auto and home repair appointments online and call local businesses for you.”

Google’s example request is “Find me a 4 p.m. nail appointment near me.” Ask Maps then shows openings at nearby businesses “so it’s easy to decide what to book,” according to the post.

Google’s demo shows Ask Maps confirming the service, location and preferred time before checking availability.

Google’s Business Profile help page on automated calls says that when customers use Google Search or Maps to connect with a business, Google might call that business on their behalf to complete the request. The requests it lists include booking appointments and confirming the price and availability of services. If a business works with online booking providers, the page says Google may book through the partner or call the business directly.

Verified businesses manage these calls in Business Profile under More, then Business Profile settings, then Advanced settings. The section labeled “Google automated calls and text messages” has a toggle for “Bookings and inquiries from customers.” A business can also ask a Google caller to stop calling.

The help page says these calls are available in every U.S. state except Indiana, Louisiana, Minnesota, Montana and Nebraska.

Google has called local businesses for searchers before. In July 2025, I covered the rollout of AI calling in Search, where people searching for a service such as auto repair or a pet groomer can tap “Have AI check pricing” and have Google call several providers nearby. Google’s help page for that feature says the person then gets an email with quotes.

When it launched in Search, a Google spokesperson said the AI picks which businesses to contact based on traditional local search rankings. Google’s Ask Maps post doesn’t say how Ask Maps chooses businesses to check or call.

At I/O in May, Google said people could ask it to call businesses “for select categories like home repair, beauty or pet care.” Three of the four Ask Maps categories match those examples.

Google’s Ask Maps post says the chat is starting to expand to 30 countries across Europe, including Spain, Germany and the U.K., bringing it to more than 200 countries and territories. Itineraries and saved-list search are available everywhere Ask Maps is offered, while appointment finding starts in the U.S.

Ask Maps puts openings from nearby businesses in front of a customer in the same conversation where they pick a place to book. For beauty, pet care, auto and home-repair businesses in the U.S., that’s a new place to win an appointment, and Ask Maps can call them to check openings.

The “Bookings and inquiries from customers” toggle in Business Profile is the control Google documents for calls it makes for customers through Search and Maps. Check where yours is set, and let whoever answers your phone know these calls come from Google on a customer’s behalf.

Google says more regions are coming soon for Ask Maps’ appointment finding, though the post names none and gives no date. Watch the Business Profile help page for word on whether the “Bookings and inquiries from customers” toggle and the five-state exclusion cover Ask Maps’ calls.

#7400. Facebook shelves additional profile option

Let Social Media Today's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

Facebook added the ability to create multiple personas in 2023, but is sunsetting the feature and deleting extra profiles by mid-December.

Meta is removing the option to create additional Facebook profiles that can be managed under a single user presence.

Which, it’s important to note, is different from creating a profile page and a business page. Users can still run business pages in addition to their individual presence. The change only relates to the alternate profile option Meta launched in 2023.

As explained by Meta: “Additional Facebook profiles are being permanently deleted after December 14, 2026. This does not affect your main Facebook profile, which is the first profile you create when you sign up for Facebook.”

As noted, in September 2023, Facebook added a multi-profile option, which enabled users to create additional Facebook profiles, in order to explore different interests or share different content with different audiences.

As Meta explained at launch: “Whether you’re new to Facebook or a longtime user, you may want to keep your personal and professional relationships separate, or you may want to keep one profile tied to a community you’re a part of and another profile just for friends. Creating multiple personal profiles lets you easily organize who you share with and what content you see for the various parts of your life. Think one profile for the foodie scene you love and another one to keep up with your friends and family.”

Though even when it was added, it did seem like a confusing and potentially harmful proposal.

As SMT reported at the time: “[Users] will have to switch over to another profile for each, which I just don’t see becoming a habitual behavior for most users, and really, it seems more likely to invite negative behaviors, like trolling, via a separate identity.”

Indeed, creating a new profile, and regularly switching between profiles, seemed more likely to add friction, while it could also be used as another means to target other people or groups via an alternate persona.

Either way, it seems that Facebook users weren’t overly interested, which is why the company is now shelving the option.

Meta said users can export their additional profile information, and those who joined groups under an alternate persona will need to rejoin under their main profile.

“If your additional profile manages a group, reassign group administration to a main profile,” Meta said. “You may also be able to add your additional profile’s connections to your main profile by adding friends, rejoining groups, or following Pages.”

Meta also said that if a user’s additional profile is an admin of a Facebook group, they’ll need to assign another profile as admin before December 14. “If no new admin is assigned, the group will be paused until an admin is added,” Meta said.
