#7370. Commerce media networks: 6 questions agencies should ask before investing

Commerce media networks (CMNs) use first-party data, media, and audience relationships across platforms to help brands reach new groups and measure outcomes across the shopping journey. Retail media networks (RMNs) are a familiar, retail-focused part of this broader landscape, and many agencies still use RMN as shorthand for the category.

“The biggest benefit of a commerce media network is that it connects the brand to their consumers at that moment of purchase when there is already intent,” said Deb Bhattacherjee, industry manager of agency partnerships at DoorDash.

As the number of commerce media networks expands and agencies play a larger role in planning and executing brand campaigns, evaluating potential partners requires looking beyond the scale of the audience and available formats to determine which networks can deliver significant growth.

Here are six questions agencies should ask when assessing the next generation of network options.

A commerce network’s greatest opportunity lies in influencing what shoppers buy, even without a specific product or brand in mind. It’s an area where DoorDash Ads shines, Bhattacherjee said.

“About two-thirds of DoorDash users[1] haven’t decided what they’re going to order,” she said. “That offers an ideal moment for brands to use storytelling to help someone discover a brand or product they may not otherwise have purchased.”

For example, a stretched parent who opens the app to order art supplies for a class project may also remember they need beauty essentials for an upcoming business trip, then add on a fun dessert for that evening — all additional purchase occasions they hadn’t originally planned.

“You want to make sure the platform is friendly for discoverability across the browsing and purchasing journey, inviting shoppers to consider your brand when they might not have originally done so both in the moment and for purchases down the road,” Bhattacherjee said.

Given the plethora of options, the question is whether the network is contributing to the existing media plan or able to offer distinct, incremental reach. Agencies should take into account not only the scale of a network’s audience but also whether it reaches unique consumers their clients aren’t already engaging through other channels.

DoorDash combines broad platform scale with the potential for incremental reach. At year-end 2025, it reported more than 56 million monthly active users[2], more than half of which are estimated to be millennials and Gen Z[3]. As of June 2026, across DoorDash, Wolt, and Deliveroo, its platforms support more than 400,000 advertisers. DoorDash also cited a June 2026 LiveRamp analysis in which more than 80% of consumers reached through its campaigns were new to advertisers’ customer bases, suggesting the platform can help brands reach beyond their existing customers into a differentiated audience.

Today’s marketer needs to prove the value of every dollar, making incremental return on ad spend (iROAS) more critical than ever. Yet according to a report from eMarketer and TransUnion, just 52% of brand and agency marketers measure their campaigns with incrementality testing.

While closed-loop attribution can link ad exposure to purchases, incrementality testing goes further by identifying sales that only happened because of the advertising. That distinction helps agencies demonstrate the true contribution of their campaigns.

Bhattacherjee said agencies should look for partners that are working toward a standardized, transparent approach to measuring incrementality. “We pursued Incrementality Certification from the Alliance for Audited Media because standardization is essential to building trust in measurement. Independent review helps establish a clear, credible foundation for how incrementality is evaluated, so agencies can better understand how metrics are calculated and what’s included. It also gives us a stronger basis for building shared learning frameworks with agency partners across first- and third-party measurement, and clean room measurement where feasible.”

Even the most promising media opportunity can lose its appeal if activating and managing campaigns adds unnecessary complexity, which is why a network should integrate into existing processes and buying strategies.

Flexibility is essential because different agencies and brands have different requirements. A network might offer managed-service options, a self-serve platform that allows buyers to directly activate and manage campaigns, or demand-side platform (DSP) that support programmatic buying. API connectivity with third-party commerce media platforms such as Pacvue and Skai can also simplify campaign management by allowing agencies to work within tools they already use.

The goal is to reduce the operational burden so agency teams can spend more time optimizing performance and developing strategy.

Current capabilities are only part of the equation. Agencies should also consider how a network is investing in technologies that can improve both the consumer shopping experience and streamline campaign management to deliver stronger results over time.

Bhattacherjee pointed to DoorDash’s AI assistant, which she said among consumers who placed grocery orders both with and without using Ask DoorDash, their average Ask grocery order had nearly 50% higher basket value than their average non-Ask grocery order, according to orders placed in August through early September 2026.

On the advertising side, DoorDash Ads continues to expand its automated bidding capabilities on sponsored products, using machine learning to optimize bids in real time. Newer enhancements allow advertisers to set minimum ROAS targets and optimize for sales while maintaining control over their campaign strategies — leading to averages of +30% attributed sales and +20% ROAS, according to internal DoorDash Ads data[4].

Agencies should also prioritize having a voice in how those tools evolve. Bhattacherjee shared that her team recently worked with an agency representing a major CPG brand that wanted to learn more about its auto-bidding solution. During the call, the agency identified what was working and suggested potential improvements, feedback that DoorDash Ads brought directly to its engineering team.

“With agencies’ eyes on our solutions, we can build our AI optimizations together to ensure they are user-friendly and easy for them to adopt, while, of course, driving performance and connecting back to broader measurement goals,” Bhattacherjee said.

Technology can make campaign execution easier, but agencies also need partners who bring strategic thinking to the table. That means looking for networks that offer proactive recommendations and opportunities for joint business planning, rather than just providing access to advertising inventory.

Bhattacherjee said the most effective partnerships allow a commerce media network to function as an extension of the agency’s team, combining proprietary insights with the agency’s understanding of the brand and its goals.

“DoorDash makes fantastic insights available, from audience-level to retailer-level data, but our clients appreciate that we synthesize that data and collaborate to convert those insights into storytelling moments,” Bhattacherjee said. “Technology alone isn’t the answer anymore, with the human touch becoming more valuable than ever. We see that agencies prioritize access to a team equipped to bring big ideas and brainstorm together.”

[1] DoorDash Consumables Study, June 2026

[2] "Monthly active users are based on the number of individual consumer accounts that completed an order on our marketplaces in the last month of the period of measurement."

[3] Numerator Advanced Shopper Profile; 12ME ending 1/31/26

[4] Average performance based on internal tests for merchants running smart campaigns from September - October, 2025

#7368. X tests adding professional histories to user profiles

Let Social Media Today's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The platform’s latest experiment with a work experience element is reminiscent of its previous attempt to build out X Jobs two years ago.

X may be gearing up to take on LinkedIn once again, with the platform currently testing professional profiles that let users list their career history.

As shown in these example images, posted on Threads by app researcher Radu Oncescu, X is experimenting with a new “work experience” element, which allows users to add their work history to their X profile.

This is no real surprise, given that X has been working to build out its job listings and professional insights graph for some time. That said, X hasn’t done much on this front for the last couple of years.

In May 2023, X owner Elon Musk hinted that X might be looking to integrate job listings as part of his broader “everything app” vision for the platform. X then launched job ad listings for verified organizations in the app in August that year, which was viewed as the platform’s first step towards facilitating job ads and candidate discovery.

In June 2024, X reported that more than 750,000 open roles had been listed in the app, less than six months after X Jobs was launched.

But two years later, the X Hiring profile in the app has gone dormant, and its dedicated job search option no longer functions.

Evidence would suggest that X simply lost interest in this element. However, with a new push to add professional histories to user profiles, maybe the platform is looking to revive that effort and re-engage job seekers in order to connect them with brands that had previously shown interest in its job market options.

The more skeptical view could be that X is only adding job listings on user profiles so it can extract more data insights, which could then be fed into xAI’s servers for expanded audience insight.

X hasn’t made any official announcement of the option either way, but it is interesting to note the platform’s apparent resurgence in interest on this front.

#7367. The future of CTV lies in standardization

Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit

Jessica Cobbe, svp, product – supply platform, Nexxen

For years, advertisers have focused primarily on in-stream video in CTV, treating the smart TV home screen as secondary real estate. But that dynamic is quickly changing, as this year’s NewFronts made clear. As viewers spend more time navigating content recommendations and streaming apps before pressing play, the home screen is becoming one of the highest-attention environments in media. The challenge here is that the infrastructure surrounding it still feels stuck in the past, lacking both nuance and standardization.

As CTV enters its next phase of growth, however, standardization will become one of the most important priorities shaping its future.

Unlike other digital or programmatic channels, native CTV inventory (including the home screen) has historically varied widely across device manufacturers, from creative specifications and ad formats to click actions and activation workflows. In practice, this means advertisers and agencies are forced to navigate a patchwork of technical requirements to achieve scaled reach. Consequently, adoption has been relatively slow, not because marketers question the value of this inventory, but because operational complexity often outweighs the benefits.

Without standardized industry specifications, preparing one native CTV campaign for multiple OEM environments can easily require 10 to 30-plus hours of prelaunch adaptation. For a single native CTV campaign, advertisers and creative teams may need to adapt the same asset package across 10 to 15 or more unique placements before launch. When dimensions, UI requirements, copy limits, image recomposition, QA and more complex executions like animated or pause ads all vary by environment, that work can add up quickly.

Worse yet, inconsistency impacts creative quality. The more time teams spend reworking assets for each environment, the harder it becomes to maintain a unified brand experience across touchpoints. Campaigns perform best when creative is designed intentionally for a given environment while still delivering consistency across the broader media plan, and standardization helps create the technical foundation that makes this possible.

Fragmented infrastructure also creates barriers to broader programmatic activation. Many buyers and planners expect the same efficiencies from CTV native inventory that they already experience across other digital channels, like display (think: streamlined workflows and scale). When inventory requires excessive customization or manual execution, it becomes harder to integrate naturally into a broader media strategy.

Standardization is not about reducing differentiation among OEMs. Rather, it’s about creating the connective tissue that allows advertisers to participate more efficiently across the ecosystem, and that efficiency benefits everyone involved. Advertisers gain simpler activation and more scalable reach. Creative teams can spend less time adapting assets and more time focusing on storytelling. Agencies can integrate native CTV inventory more seamlessly into omnichannel planning. And OEMs can make their inventory more accessible to a broader range of buyers.

As the CTV market continues to mature, operational simplicity is becoming just as important as premium supply. And for smart TV home screens, standardization may prove to be the unlock that moves this inventory from a promising opportunity to an outcome-driving media channel.Partner insights from Nexxen

#7365. How CeraVe’s ‘Dune’ deal takes the brand’s social-first playbook global

The L’Oréal brand’s first film partnership makes it the “Official Moisturizer of Arrakis” ahead of the blockbuster’s Dec. 18 release.

CeraVe last week partnered with “Dune: Part Three” to become the “Official Moisturizer of Arrakis,” the desert planet that serves as the sci-fi epic’s titular setting. The tie-up with Warner Bros. Pictures and Legendary Pictures represents the L'Oréal brand’s first film partnership, with a campaign that will roll out ahead of the movie’s Dec. 18 theatrical release.

The brand on Monday revealed the next chapter in the campaign. A humorous “Sandworm Wrangler” video, shot in the style of behind-the-scenes content, shows how a wrangler of one of the film’s iconic sandworms uses CeraVe Moisturizing Cream — which now offers 120 hours of hydration — on the dry-skinned creature.

The debut “Precious Resource” spot reimagined the lore of Arrakis, an arid planet where every drop of moisture is preserved, replacing the story’s central resource, spice, with CeraVe. The “Dune” partnership is the latest iteration of a “medutainment” strategy that combines science with entertainment and has helped grow CeraVe into a $2 billion brand.

“When it comes to the playbook, that's something we are reproducing here with ‘Dune,’” said Vincent Chauvière, global brand president at CeraVe. “It's a multipoint campaign that is social-first, starting with a bit of excitement and surprise, and then we are going full media.”

Along with co-branded content, the campaign spans paid, earned, social, digital, retail, creator and experiential activations. The brand will also launch out-of-home ads, creator gifting and corporate screening experiences, as well as sponsor film premiere events in Los Angeles and the U.K.

“Our goal is to create partnerships that extend the worlds of our films in ways that feel unexpected, culturally relevant and genuinely entertaining,” Julie Moore, executive vice president, global brand partnerships at Warner Bros. Pictures, said in a statement.

The “Dune” campaign was created and produced by OBB Bolded, OBB’s branded content studio, with content filmed in Samalayuca Dunes in Mexico and Mexico City and directed by Maca Rubio from Stink Films. OBB was also behind an award-winning “Moisturize Like a Derm” effort that appointed NBA star Kevin Durant as the brand’s “Face of Legs.”

“It's been a campaign that has been working at bringing awareness to the brand, but also to the usage of a body moisturizer, bringing our science to new consumers, particularly men. We've been recruiting more men this year, thanks to this partnership [with the NBA],” Chauvière explained.

The “Dune” partnership is rolling out globally, and the campaign is designed to pair content around the billion-dollar franchise with market-specific dermatologists and experiential activations. CeraVe is growing at a double-digit rate this year and gaining share around the world, and geographic expansion is key to the brand’s future growth, Chauvière said.

“The partnership with ‘Dune’ [is] a way to have a more consistent brand tone of voice and point of view. We have local teams that have a lot of local activations, and the influencer world is a local world. So it's all all about the balance,” the executive said.

The local push builds on CeraVe’s larger creator strategy, which helps the brand reach more than 15 million followers across platforms. The brand this summer united over 100 creators from 22 countries for its first Global CerAwards in Los Angeles. The event included CeraVe Studios, an immersive content creation experience hosted on a Hollywood studio lot, that generated nearly 60 million views of new content, per Chauvière.

“It was a moment of visibility, but it's also a moment to gather all the local influencers together and reunite around this idea of bringing creativity in the beauty world and making science accessible and entertaining at the same time,” the executive said.

#7364. ‘We’re not trying to be TwitchTok’: Twitch adds new short-form video feature

Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit

For Twitch streamers, on-platform discoverability has always been a major issue. Twitch has tried to address this, with mixed success. Now, the platform is making its biggest swing yet.

Starting early next year, Twitch will let creators upload short-form videos made outside the platform. Announced during the keynote at TwitchCon 2026 in San Diego, the move is aimed at improving on-platform discovery and creating more ad inventory. Twitch’s goal isn’t to make clips into a TikTok-like destination, execs say, but to help viewers discover creators and tune into their livestreams, where creators make most of their money.

The new uploads build on Twitch’s existing Clips tools, which have let creators and viewers clip livestreams and share them on-platform for more than a decade. But clips made or shared outside the platform are now a central part of creator culture.

“It’s a smart thing for them to do. You want to follow your favorite Twitch creators but you aren’t able to catch them live at that moment, so you’re going to TikTok or you’re watching old uploads on YouTube,” said Eric Bogard, CEO of UnderCurrent Talent.

Cross-platform follower conversion is difficult, especially for streamers. “Every data point will always show you that getting people to click over different platforms doesn’t work really at all,” said Tim McArdle, co-founder and chief content officer at creative studio Wildcatter.

Twitch’s chief product officer Mike Minton said the platform had “missed an opportunity” to make clips happen on Twitch. Historically, Twitch creators’ short-form content goes viral on TikTok, X, YouTube Shorts, and Instagram, racking up millions of views.

McArdle said that, though Twitch is a bit behind the game, these features could fundamentally change the platform. “They needed to do it, and for a company that produces a lot on Twitch, we’re excited about it,” he said.

Twitch streamers Vio and Frogan were less optimistic about the new short-form push. “People don’t go to Twitch to find clips or videos. They go to YouTube or TikTok,” said Vio. “They need to let the Clips thing go. No one is going to watch clips on Twitch natively,” said Frogan. Dan “Onepeg” Marshall, who has over 72,000 followers on the platform, said it’s a good move for the overall ethos of Twitch.

Twitch already has an existing “Clips” tab on both its mobile and desktop versions, but it will also add a new “Category Recap” shelf that will appear on category pages, which will populate with clips and recaps. Marshall found the Category Recaps the most interesting feature announced, noting it could be a positive for creators in specific categories trying to catch eyeballs.

“Of all of the things Twitch has tried to pull in the last several years, this is probably one of the better ideas for discoverability if it does more than just show clips of the largest creators in each category,” he said.

With this investment in short-form content, Twitch feeds will eventually become more personalized for users, whose viewing habits will dictate whether they’re fed more short-form content or more streams, according to Minton.

“We’re not trying to be TwitchTok,” he clarified. Instead, Twitch hopes these new features will help creators get discovered on-platform, which will make it easier to funnel viewers into livestreams, which is where they make their money.

“Will people consume as much of the clips on Twitch as TikTok? Probably not, but that’s OK… the utility of why they’re doing it and how it’s going to be used is different,” said McArdle.

Twitch’s new editing tools will make it easier to find exciting moments and turn them into clips. That could be a boon for smaller creators who don’t have the money to hire an editor or the time to edit content on an external app or program after they’ve been livestreaming for hours. Vio and Marshall wondered whether AI would power these features. Vio said the existing AI tools have been “ass so far.”

Minton told Digiday he’s focused on the “torso and long tail of creators” on Twitch. A more robust creator platform with better discoverability means more creators making money.

Allowing creators to upload externally made clips, rather than just chopped up, unedited versions of their streams, adds even more inventory to the platform. “It sounds like they’re trying to capture more inventory as leverage from an advertising perspective,” said Justin Miclat, chief growth officer at talent and brand management company Click Media.

Minton said increased audiences are what advertisers care about, and that Clips can help activations organized directly between brands and creators.

For creators however, the advertiser opportunity won’t yet translate into direct revenue. Minton confirmed that, though there are ads nestled amongst clips, there’s no direct monetization for short-form on Twitch just yet.

“Twitch is mostly live monetization, so the transition from the short form into live is where you’re going to make your money,” Minton said. “70 percent of it directly from your fans versus ad-supported. I do think over time we will find ways for ads in and around clips that’ll make sense that won’t diminish the user experience but will increase those earning opportunities for creators.”

Ultimately, this short-form push should help content creators on Twitch get more eyes on their livestreams, a notoriously difficult task the platform has been struggling with for years.

“Live content isn’t amazing for discovery… You hop into [a stream], you may not understand what’s going on. It could be a dead moment in a stream, it’s just not great,” Minton said. “Whereas short form is amazing…you get a snapshot of a great moment, and you can decide: ‘Is this something I want to spend more time on?’ Yes, it is. Follow. Boom. Next time you open up the app, that streamer’s in the feed.”

#7363. Instagram launches iPhone Duo-native app

Let Social Media Today's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The new version features functions specifically designed to take advantage of the device’s larger screen.

Instagram has launched a dedicated iPhone Duo version of its app that uses the device’s expanded display capacity to enable more on-screen functions.

As shown in this example image, the main Instagram feed will open to a wider presentation format, with more room on the screen.

For Reels, the Duo version of IG will display posts and comments in a side-by-side view, which will make it easier to view both elements.

As explained by Instagram: “When your phone is open, you can read comments beside a full-size Reel. The video keeps playing while you read along, so you can follow the conversation without shrinking what you’re watching.”

Instagram added that it’s moved the control buttons to the sidebar, which will leave more space for photos and videos.

“When your phone is folded, Instagram Stories and Reels keep their familiar vertical format,” Instagram said.

Messages and notifications will open into a two-column layout, with the inbox display on one side and highlighted exchanges on the other.

The custom presentation format could provide new opportunities for engagement and interaction in the app by making it easier for users to view content and see the related comments on a single screen.

That could also provide some interesting content considerations for creators, although this display format is restricted to Duo users only, which is a limiting factor.

Either way, this is a new view for Instagram, which aligns with Apple’s latest display approach.

Instagram also launched a Duo version of its Edits app last week.

#7361. Deloitte Digital takes the holdco operating system pitch straight to the CEO

Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit

CEOs have never cared much for holdcos. Enterprise solutions, on the other hand, get a meeting. Which makes Deloitte Digital’s new operating system for marketers an awkward one for the rest of the industry.

It’s sold as a license, though not the kind a CMO can approve alone. Designed eventually to stretch across sales, marketing, service and commerce, it’s the kind of deal Deloitte Digital’s U.S. CMO Mark Singer called a “more executive conversation.” That conversation happens in the C-suite, well above the marketing department where holdcos usually pitch.

The product is called Converge Front Office. It strings together AI agents, some built by Deloitte and others a client already runs elsewhere, to handle marketing and sales work from research and briefs through to campaign deployment and deal tracking. Two parts are live, a marketing operating system and a sales one, with a commerce version on the way. Singer pitched them as pieces of one front office system built around an idea the consulting firm calls “brand to cash” — every step of marketing and sales, from building a brand to closing a deal, should be traceable back to revenue.

“It’s not just about the agents, it’s about the task orchestration among them,” said Singer.

If that sounds familiar, it’s because holdcos have spent the better part of two years saying much the same. It carries more weight from a consulting firm, though, and Singer made a point of setting Deloitte’s version apart. The market is full of AI tools, he said, and “everybody’s doing a press release every 20 minutes on them.” Some exist to make an agency more efficient for its cleints. Others sell smarter work off the back of an owner’s media insights. Deloitte wants to build tools “that we hand off to our clients,” said Singer. From there, they can run them in-house or use them as a way of “rethinking their agency infrastructure,” he added.

A demo showed how that could play out. Umberto Castaldo, Deloitte Digital’s Converge marketing go-to-market lead, ran a campaign for a dummy sneaker brand. Agents passed the work along from market research and media modelling to the brief, the content, quality assurance and finally deployment into the brand’s existing mar tech. All those agents are routed into the consulting firm’s wider tech stack. Some of them draw on Deloitte’s own asset along the way. The research agent, for instance, can tap Deloitte’s own third-party data spine alongside client data.

Of those steps, content is doing a fair share of the selling, at least in the system’s current form. In the consulting firm’s view, brands have already paid for far more content than they’ve used.

Big brands have spent hundreds of millions, if not billions, on content over the past five years, Castaldo argued, and little of it has run recently. The system’s answer is to put that back catalog to work. Tagging agents can first relabel what sits in a brand’s asset library so other agents can find it. In the demo, those agents then built email and display ads for three audiences out of images and headlines the sneaker brand already had on file. Each asset is tracked from there, so the brand can see how it performs from one campaign to the next.

The sales side runs in parallel. Abe Awasthi, Deloitte Digital’s AI sales transformation leader, showed how its built around a seller’s day: the gap to quote, which deals need attention and where new demand might come from. That last job falls to an agent called Scout, which reads campaign results from the marketing side and matches them to a rep’s target customers. Administrators decide how far each agent can go, from suggesting to drafting to acting.

“Autonomy should be earned,” said Awasthi.

For now, most early clients are using the two halves separately, though Singer said some are starting to take both. Joint marketing and sales deals remain early, with one or two pitches in the past year, Singer said. As clients mature, he expects them to see the value in the “white space in between.”

The consulting firm shared one result. A client gave half of its 300 business development reps the sales operating system. Over a three-month pilot, the response rate on their outbound emails went from 17% to around 56%. Once the rollout scaled, that settled in the 30s — roughly double the starting point. Quotas for the team up 20%, said Awasthi, and the client is hiring more reps. Marketing teams are similarly seeing early gains in throughput, said Castaldo, who didn’t share any specifics.

Like everything the consulting firm has tried in advertising, Converge is designed to sit above it all, and Singer was blunt about where that leads. He expects “everything will be disrupted” across marketing services and said the shift is already underway. Four large clients he wouldn’t name are pulling their marketing into global capability centers, which he said is now possible without losing the personalization each market and language needs. Deloitte Digital already runs centralized functions like these for clients. They cover most of the marketing work, though brand advertising sits outside them. Setting up a function on that scale. Singer added, means building what he called “captive environments” for it.

In outsourcing, a “captive” is an operation a company owns and runs for itself. The brand keeps the people and the budget. The system they all work inside is another matter, and that’s what the largest marketing services groups are now chasing. Consulting firms like Deloitte have the advantage of already being in the room where that gets decided. The holdcos have been trying to get there for a while. At CES in January, Omnicom, Stagwell, Havas and WPP each unveiled agentic platforms built to sit on top of a client’s existing tools and run the work between them. WPP has since gone further, recasting itself as a single company with four divisions: WPP Media, WPP Production, WPP Enterprise Solutions and the newly-created WPP Creative. Publicis started earlier, paying $3.5 billion for Sapient in 2015 and $4.4 billion for Epsilon in 2019. Software companies are doing the same. Adobe used its conference earlier this month to introduce its end-to-end content supply chain product.

“One of the secret weapons of the management consultancy agencies in gaining market share during the past 10 years has been leveraging their established relationships with client CEOs, CIOs, and Boards of Directors,” said Gartner vp analyst Jay Wilson. “These relationships, and the credibility and sway those agencies have with those executives often allowed them to intercept opportunities before an agency review took place. Increasingly, we see and hear from clients and agencies that the CFO is the critical piece of the new business puzzle, as marketing budgets remain flat, and CMOs are pressured to prove the value of marketing, including agency investments.”

#7359. Amazon puts Arnold Schwarzenegger in Santa suit to extend holiday push

A new spot ties into the upcoming movie “The Man with the Bag,” showing Amazon again tapping into its own programming to promote its range of offerings.

Amazon is once again tapping into its Prime ecosystem to integrate one of its entertainment properties into an advertising campaign. Taking inspiration from “The Man with the Bag,” which premiers Dec. 2, the e-commerce platform has created a light-hearted holiday ad featuring a familiar face.

“Santa Schwarzenegger” follows the actor as he uses a Santa suit, delivered by Prime, to explore New York City unnoticed. During his adventure, Schwarzenegger is able to watch a game with bar patrons, catch a holiday movie and use his strength to help a family get a Christmas tree on the roof of their car. It ends with the actor using an Amazon Locker to pick up a pair of skates so he can enjoy time on an ice rink. The minute-long spot is set to “Make Someone Happy” by Jimmy Durante.

Schwarzenegger will also appear as Santa throughout the season outside of the spot and movie, per press details.

Amazon has made finding moments of joy a central part of its holiday strategy. “Santa Schwarzenegger” follows the longer “Joy Delivered” spot, which tells the story of a young woman going on a “Planes, Trains and Automobiles”-style journey to make it home to her family in time for the holidays, giving away the gifts she bought along the way.

This is not the first time Amazon has drawn inspiration from a Prime Video title in its advertising. In May, Amazon’s Brand Innovation Lab released a spot with Liquid I.V. featuring the leading actors from its hockey romance show, “Off Campus,” marking the first time Prime Video leads appeared in a co-branded spot.

“Santa Schwarzenegger” allows the e-commerce giant to promote its delivery services while also showing how its properties can be used for advertising.

Amazon’s ad revenue hit $19.6 billion in Q3, a 12% year-over-year increase, per an earnings statement. However, this is a significant dip from the 26% YoY growth rate seen just a quarter earlier, leading to a stock dip for the company.

#7358. How Bustle Digital Group is helping Pampers and Innisfree show up in AI recommendations

Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit

Bustle Digital Group is using Profound’s AI measurement tools to help brands, including Pampers and Innisfree, show up in AI-generated recommendations.

The publisher’s GEO offering, called ECHO internally, uses Profound analytics and AI agents trained on content from BDG’s titles to generate creative briefs and guidelines. BDG’s creative team uses those materials to produce content designed to be cited by AI platforms. At least three brands have paid for the offering.

An uptick in client inquiries this year prompted BDG to develop the offering, said Graham Howes, svp of distribution and AI intelligence at BDG, which owns titles like Bustle, Nylon, Elite Daily and Scary Mommy.

BDG is the only publisher currently working with Profound to turn this process into an advertiser offering.

In one campaign, which ran between Aug 11–Sep 30, Korean beauty brand Innisfree’s visibility across 200 tracked skincare prompts grew 30%, while Bustle’s citation rank rose from #709 to #12, according to a BDG case study based on Profound data.

“By combining trusted editorial environments, answer engine optimization, and prompt-level measurement, we were able to demonstrate that AI visibility can be measured, optimized, and ultimately transformed into a meaningful competitive advantage,” said Julien Bouzitat, gm of Innisfree U.S., part of the Amore Pacific Group.

Baby care brand Pampers moved from #2 to #1 in AI visibility for fragrance-free diaper questions following a Scary Mommy explainer addressing Swaddlers’ fragrance-free switch. The explainer ran between Sep 4–17.

“There isn’t a defined playbook for how publishers should be approaching this. So we really had to come at this from a very DIY place of first understanding the space,” Howes said.

The process begins with an RFP and conversations with the brand on their AI visibility goals, Howes explained. Then comes a two- to four-week baseline research phase, where BDG and Profound analyze eight to 10 topics that the advertiser wants to increase its visibility against within an AI answer engine, and 25 to 50 prompts [on each topic] to understand the brand’s competitive standing and what sites the answer engines are currently citing.

BDG then uses its own AI agents, trained on its titles’ content, to develop an editorial strategy for the branded content. This includes potential article topics, headline structure, and tone, Howes explained. That strategy is then presented to the advertiser.

“The advertiser has no hand in the actual creative development at all. We leave that entirely up to our editors, partly because we want to make sure that we are following all of the best practices of what gets cited, and something that is very heavy-handed on the advertorial front is very unlikely to do that,” Howes said.

AI agents within Profound then design the creative briefs, which get handed off to BDG’s creative team. They write in their own voice, but follow guidelines set by the agents, such as including an FAQ section at the bottom of the article, or the type of article format, such as a listicle or an explainer.

“You’ve got to be able to connect analytics into action,” said Josh Blyskal, head of insights at Profound.

Once the content is live, it’s cross-promoted on Reddit, where BDG is running paid media. This helps build awareness among relevant communities of Reddit users, which “still matters a lot in the overall algorithm of what is being picked up and why,” Howes said. Reddit, he added, remains a significant citation source for answer engines.”

BDG tracks the performance of those posts throughout the campaign, he added.

This is the big question, especially given attribution is difficult because AI platforms offer limited insight into how people use their answers to make purchasing decisions, making it hard for publishers to attribute AI’s influence on traffic, engagement and conversions.

BDG tracks the performance of the GEO-branded content by analyzing metrics including the brand’s visibility on AI platforms, and BDG’s citation share and citation rank, mainly across ChatGPT, Gemini and Google’s AI Overviews.

Profound measures AI visibility by whether the brand appears in an AI response. Citation share measures the percentage of total citations in a given set of AI-generated answers that come from a particular publisher’s site, Blyskal said. (Citation share is typically between 0.1% and 3%, he noted.) Citation rank measures how a publisher’s content ranks against competitors based on how frequently each is cited in AI-generated answers.

“We want to really be able to prove to the best of our ability, that these two goals are interconnected when we run programs in this kind of way,” Howes said.

Using Profound, BDG identifies examples of its content appearing in AI answers, monitors which articles generate the most citations and makes real-time optimizations to improve performance, Howes said. Advertisers then receive a report detailing the results.

“Now the question is, does the influence layer – i.e., ChatGPT, where people find the conviction to decide what to buy – net cleanly into the transaction layer, which is often through Google into the website? And the answer is no, not right now,” Blyskal said.

Howes declined to share how much revenue its GEO offering was generating, or how much BDG was charging brands for this offering. It’s sold as a standalone offering, or bundled into existing custom content packages. Profound does not receive a cut of these deals.

“We see this more as an extension of [our] custom content opportunities, not a replacement to them,” Howes said. “Clients can still have those opportunities to reach our audiences on our sites, on our social channels, but also pair that with these types of opportunities to also reach similar audiences that are now choosing to engage an answer engine to have a question answered.”

Ashish Jacob, director of GEO at Go Fish Digital, said consistent measurement matters more than which analytics platforms a company uses to track visibility.

“The most valuable metrics include how often a brand appears in relevant AI responses, which sources are cited, sentiment, competitive share of voice, and how those results change over time. It’s also important to understand the prompts, AI platforms, and sampling methods behind the data, since different tools may produce different results. First-party reporting is becoming increasingly valuable as well,” Jacob said.

Profound is seeing some renewals for 2027, as well as exploring running always-on, yearlong campaigns, Howes said.

“A lot of advertisers realize that this content is very powerful, but it also has a half-life to it, and if you want to really make sure that you have an ongoing presence – especially when we think about our partners in beauty and fashion, where so much of what they’re doing is very seasonal – that they need to really have a more always-on approach to their content strategy,” Howes said.

These GEO offerings require publishers to be nimble, Howes said. Because AI answer engines are constantly changing their algorithms, GEO requires ongoing monitoring, research and content optimization, he said. Publishers must continually adapt their strategies to keep brands visible in AI-generated answers. But that’s an opportunity in itself, to act “not just as content partners” but as “a knowledge resource” to help brands understand what’s happening within AI answer engine recommendations, he added.

Howes sees GEO as an opportunity not just to improve its own visibility in AI search, but to grow its advertising business. Branded and custom content is BDG’s largest revenue source, he said. Measuring and demonstrating how GEO efforts benefit advertisers will be critical to strengthening brand partnerships and expanding these offerings as a revenue stream, Howes noted.

“I really want to better understand how this new paradigm we find ourselves in really plays a direct role in our business, not just our own editorial growth. To be able to have that kind of data and visibility, not just in our own efforts, but in our advertisers’ efforts as well, is fundamental to what we do because we need to be able to have that level of transparency to grow the kind of partnerships that we’re looking to grow into next year with these types of packages,” Howes said.

#7356. Software Engineer - AI Tooling Infrastructure at Supabase

Supabase is the Postgres development platform, built by developers for developers. We provide a complete backend solution including Database, Auth, Storage, Edge Functions, Realtime, and Vector Search. All services are deeply integrated and designed for growth.

We’re looking for a Software Engineer, AI Tooling Infrastructure to join our AI Tooling team and help build and run the backend services behind Supabase’s AI products. The Supabase MCP server is one example of what the team runs in production, alongside the services that support agent skills and the dashboard assistant. You’ll work closely with the Platform, SRE, Auth, Billing and Edge Functions teams, and with the engineers on the AI Tooling team who build the product surfaces.

The AI Tooling team runs its own services in production and carries its own on-call. Traffic from AI clients and agents behaves differently from traffic from people: hundreds of calls a minute, retry loops, and no reading of deprecation warnings. This role makes sure the services they use are reliable, correctly authorized and observable. It is a systems and infrastructure role rather than a product AI role, and it is not an SRE role. You will build and operate these systems, not only advise on them.

This role is ideal for someone who thrives in async, fast-paced environments, owns what they ship in production, and is excited about building developer tools that scale to millions.

Build and operate the production backend services behind Supabase’s AI products, including the MCP server: deployment, scaling, configuration and release.

Take ownership of how those services are structured, including splitting or reshaping a service when that makes it safer to run and easier to change.

Define, measure and meet reliability targets for the services the team runs. Set SLOs with the SRE team, track error budgets, and use them to decide what to fix first.

Participate in the AI Tooling team on-call rotation, and be a first responder for incidents in those services. Investigate, fix, coordinate with other teams during incidents, and write the follow-ups and runbooks.

Work the AI Tooling team support queue alongside on-call, and turn recurring issues into fixes rather than repeated manual answers.

Own authentication and authorization for AI and agent clients: OAuth apps, scoped tokens, and permissions that make sense for agents as well as humans, including how we change or deprecate a permission without breaking existing integrations.

Own observability for the services the team runs: metrics, traces, logs, dashboards and alerts, so we find problems before customers do.

Handle capacity and abuse for agent traffic: rate limits, cost and safety controls, and behavior under load or when a dependency degrades.

Improve the architecture of the services the team owns as they grow, including splitting or reshaping a service when that makes it safer to run and easier to change.

Work with the Platform team on shared code, review ownership and release process, and with the SRE team on infrastructure, alerting and incident practice.

Contribute to the code of the AI Tooling team’s tools, such as the MCP server, where it affects reliability and security, in partnership with the engineers who own the product surface.

Have 5+ years of experience building and running backend services in production, and have carried on-call for them.

Write strong TypeScript or Go, and are comfortable working in the other.

Have designed and operated APIs with real consumers: versioning, error handling, rate limiting, and backwards-compatible change.

Know OAuth, OIDC, JWT and API authorization well enough to debug them in production and to explain where implementations commonly deviate from the spec.

Have a good understanding of PostgreSQL and relational databases.

Are comfortable with CI/CD, Docker and containerized deployments, and with infrastructure as code. Any tool is fine.

Can debug across services: follow a slow or failing request through several systems using metrics, traces and logs.

Communicate clearly in writing, work with a wide range of stakeholders, and thrive in async, globally distributed teams.

Are comfortable navigating ambiguity and moving quickly.

APIs and auth: You have designed permission models, token scopes or OAuth flows for third-party or machine clients, and you have migrated them without breaking users.

Gateways and distributed systems: You have built or run proxies or gateways, or debugged hard failures across services (retries, partial failures, upstream outages, fail-open vs fail-closed decisions), and you can reason about load and degradation.

Experience with agent tooling (MCP or similar), or serving traffic from AI agents and LLM clients.

Experience moving a service out of a larger codebase while keeping existing clients working.

Experience with Grafana, OpenTelemetry, Logflare or a similar observability stack, and real SLO work.

Open-source contributions, especially to Node.js, Go, TypeScript or API tooling.

We operate asynchronously and trust you to manage your own time. You know what needs to be done and when.

#7355. Meow Mix reimagines iconic cat memes for multichannel campaign

The J.M. Smucker Co. cat food brand fictionalized behind-the-scenes videos for internet-famous characters including Keyboard Cat and Huh Cat.

Meow Mix’s “Behind the Memeow” campaign piggybacks on popular internet cat memes that continue to be a sizeable part of internet culture — if not quite the 15% of the internet cited in press materials, a persistent figure that originated in a campaign by competitor Friskies over a decade ago.

“Cats have always had a special place in internet culture, and some of the most iconic memes of all time have come from their wonderfully unpredictable personalities,” Nicole Massey, vice president of marketing for pet products at J.M. Smucker Co, said in a statement. “With ‘Behind the Memeow,’ we’re celebrating that cultural legacy while reminding cat parents that even the pickiest, most notoriously hard-to-please cats can’t resist Meow Mix.”

Three 30-second ads feature meme characters Table Cat, Keyboard Cat and Huh Cat and show how Meow Mix changed their behavior. Each spot features new lyrics for the iconic Meow Mix jingle, which the brand has continued to iterate on to reach new generations of consumers.

Beyond the ad spots, the campaign will be amplified with a social-first media strategy that includes paid support across Meta, Pinterest, Snapchat and Reddit, with a high-impact TikTok placement. #7354. Substack job listing hints at a bigger advertising push in 2027

Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit

Few took Substack’s co-founder and chief writing officer Hamish McKenzie literally when he told Digiday in 2025 that ads were a long way off. A new job hire suggests they should have.

The online publishing and newsletter platform is currently hiring a U.S.-based product manager of payments to help expand monetization on Substack and find better ways to support paying creators, according to the company’s careers page.

The job spec states that the scope of the role includes gifting, retention offers and improvements to the payments and subscription experience, alongside opportunities to explore commerce, and (crucially) advertising-related monetization over time. The role, which comes with a cash compensation package between $210,000 and $230,000, will also help shape future ad opportunities as the business evolves.

Substack first signalled a willingness to reconsider ads in March 2025 when Digiday spoke to McKenzie. He described ads as an “interesting business” for Substack, while suggesting it was “some way off in the distant future.”

Since making those comments, Substack has gradually started taking a more active role in connecting brands with publishers, although its efforts so far have focused on sponsorships rather than conventional ads.

Historically, ads on Substack have been creator-led rather than platform-led. Brands typically partnered directly with individual newsletters or creator networks, arranging sponsorships across newsletters and podcasts.

In June, it announced the first phase of a native sponsorship program, introducing Creator Kits to help publishers showcase their audiences and attract brand partners. In October, it introduced three sponsorship formats:

But the latest job spec suggests Substack could be considering a broader role for advertising in its monetization strategy from next year.

For some, this brings both opportunities and risks. Substack’s potential pivot toward paid advertising feels like “the end of an idealistic era,” according to Brenda Imeson, director of strategy at Brave Bison. Another platform that built its identity partly around resisting ads is now facing the commercial realities of sustaining its business.

“Subscription fatigue is biting, paywalls inevitably gatekeep good journalism and limit reach. If handled sensitively, native sponsorships will allow writers to keep more work free without hollowing out editorial integrity and could democratize access to great writing,” Imeson said. “The test will be if Substack can take brand money and keep thoughtful discourse from degrading into attention grabbing algorithmic bait.”

#7352. Deloitte Digital’s new agentic tools aim to fix messy marketing workflows

A new Converge by Front Office suite is designed to help brands better connect their existing technology stacks and wring greater value from them.

Marketers continue to wrestle with the gap between the promise of AI and the reality of the technology’s results, which for some haven’t lived up to the hype. Agencies and other marketing services providers are responding to persistent frustrations around AI fragmentation and execution with a wave of solutions themed around orchestration, or improving workflows.

Seventy-six percent of surveyed brand leaders believe their operating foundations do not meaningfully support realizing value from AI, which CMOs are under growing pressure to master, according to a recent Deloitte Digital report on personalization trends. Nearly all, 97%, of respondents say that the pace of AI development outstrips their ability to optimize AI for personalization purposes. Platform and workflow inefficiencies were also cited as hindrances.

The consultancy’s Converge Front Office suite seeks to address these shortcomings by bringing greater unity to marketers’ AI tech stacks. Agents will work to link existing tools and data, including from cloud-computing and software providers. Clients can also enlist Deloitte engineers to ensure Converge solutions cater to specific needs or adapt as their organization’s priorities evolve.

The Converge Marketing product is designed to break down silos and better integrate campaign strategy, planning, execution and measurement while ensuring marketers retain control over key decisions. Agent capabilities span research, strategy planning, asset building, campaign optimization and performance tracking. The goal is to get marketers from the pilot phase to production faster, Mark Singer, marketing service lead and CMO at Deloitte Digital, said in a statement.

Converge Sales boasts agents that can help identify prospects, engage inbound buyers and manage sales pipeline activity, among other functions. Deloitte Digital is aligning the new Converge brands with Converge Signals, a predictive intelligence platform that draws on data from partners including customer insights firm HundredX and Deloitte Digital’s own BrandWorth scoring system.

Other agencies are racing to hone their competitive edge on the agentic front. Publicis Groupe recently completed its acquisition of data-collaboration platform LiveRamp, a deal the ad-holding group says will enable it to produce more sophisticated agents on behalf of clients.

Deloitte has ramped up its agentic services as some of its consulting divisions experience a slowdown. The company’s technology and transformation unit grew 2.5% in the fiscal year 2026, a lower rate of growth than the prior year.

#7351. How brands are banking on live shopping this holiday season

Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit

The story was first published by Digiday sibling Glossy

Many brands have accepted that, to effectively compete this holiday season, last year’s marketing playbook won’t cut it.

More brands are gravitating toward live shopping, a growing channel that is set to play an outsized influence on shopping trends. According to data from eMarketer, livestream retail sales in the U.S. are set to reach nearly $20 billion this year. And annual spend per buyer on livestreams is growing by 23% to an average of $339.27.

Brands like Tarte Cosmetics, Crocs, Beachwaver and Gap are planning to make use of live shopping, particularly on TikTok, this holiday season. Tarte and Crocs plan to launch exclusive products just for TikTok live shopping, with Crocs’ exclusives including a Disney collaboration. TikTok has seen livestream shopping sales double in the first half of this year, and use of the hashtag #holidayshopping rose 263% year over year in October.

Ziad Bon, founder of Oudware, the 3-year-old fragrance retailer that sells imported fragrances from the Middle East, told Glossy that live shopping has become an integral part of his company’s holiday strategy. Oudware already has a fairly comprehensive strategy, hosting live shopping shows on weekdays for its 215,000 followers. From Black Friday through mid-December, Oudware will be increasing its live frequency, going live on TikTok Shop every day from 2 p.m. to 7 p.m. EST. Oudware already makes more than $200,000 per month from live shopping on average and does more than $20 million in annual revenue. Its products sell for around $30-$100 per bottle.

Bon said it’s important for brands engaging in live shopping to have a plan for each live. Oudware’s live strategy is to spend the first hour of each live with what Bon called the “gift hotline,” where the team takes feedback and requests from viewers on which items and fragrances they want to see go on sale that evening. The next few hours are spent showcasing products and putting them up for sale through the regular TikTok Shop sales channel. The last hour or two of each live are reserved for auctions, a feature on TikTok Shop announced in 2025 and rolled out more broadly this year.

For Oudware, which sells about 3,000 products per day on TikTok Shop livestreams, saving the auctions for last is crucial. Live shopping conversion rates tend to be much higher than standard e-commerce, and consumers are increasingly drawn to auctions due to the possibility of lower prices. Adobe data from this year found that people are nearly 70% more likely to buy something during a live shopping stream if they see others bidding as well.

“Personally, I hate auctions,” Bon said. “A lot of our fragrance manufacturers don’t want their fragrances sold at auction, and the prices are often super low. But as a seller, it’s really hard to get engagement if you’re not doing auctions, since that’s what the customers want.”

Running auctions only at the end of the live has two purposes: It lets Oudware spend the majority of a livestream selling products at their regular prices and saves the auctions for when the live has the most viewers. More viewers means more bids, which means Oudware can sell products at auction for closer to the normal asking price.

Live shopping was a big success for brands last holiday season. TikTok Shop saw over $500 million in sales throughout the holiday period in 2025. Meanwhile, on Black Friday last year, Whatnot saw $75 million in sales in one day, tripling its previous peak from the year before.

TikTok itself is also introducing new features to support live shopping for the holidays. In the past year, big name brands and retailers like Fenty Beauty and Sephora have joined TikTok Shop. Products sold on a live will now have a visible badge if they’re part of TikTok’s Fulfilled by TikTok program (similar to Amazon Prime). Bon said the ability to ship product right after a live ends and have it arrive three days later is likely to be a big draw for customers. And, starting this fall, TikTok Shop will be working with Happy Returns to let shoppers return purchased items to any of Happy Returns’ 10,000 drop-off locations across the U.S.

“Live shopping has become one of the most engaging formats on TikTok Shop, and we expect even more brands to embrace it this holiday season as they look for new ways to connect with shoppers,” said Patrick Nommensen, president of strategic initiatives at TikTok Shop, in an email to Glossy. “What makes Live particularly compelling during the holidays is its ability to turn product discovery into an interactive shopping experience, allowing consumers to watch demonstrations, ask questions, and hear directly from brands and creators before making a purchase.”

#7349. Media Buying Briefing: Buyers grapple with incoming Amazon reporting changes

Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit

This Media Buying Briefing covers the latest in agency news and media buying for Digiday+ members and is distributed over email every Monday at 10 a.m. ET. More from the series →

Changes in the way that key media platforms measure impressions mean that performance and pricing benchmarks may be thrown into disarray come the new year.

Amazon has estimated brands will see 63% fewer impressions for display ads appearing across its retail properties, including its homepage, product pages and search results, according to a notice distributed among advertisers seen by Digiday. It’s due to the platform’s decision to shift from counting impressions the moment they begin downloading to a user’s device, to when they actually render on the user’s screen, from Jan. 1. Google announced a similar transition at the beginning of September, effective Feb. 17; spokespeople from both tech companies declined to comment.

In turn, six buyers who spoke to Digiday said they’re working to amend reporting methodologies and soothe client nerves.

Buyers fear that a reduction in reported impressions could mean that supply is constrained, driving up CPMs. “If there’s going to be fewer impressions, your CPMs will be higher,” explained Hannah Schatz, vp of programmatic operations at Coegi.

At the same time, the stricter impression reporting methodology means that lower-impact display placements further down Store pages will become even less desirable for advertisers — while top-of-page slots that stand a greater chance of influencing shoppers will see an increase in demand.

“There’s going to be probably more competition on the platform,” said Nola Ladd, awareness media supervisor at media agency Collective Measures.

Amazon has not issued guidance regarding the expected impact on pricing or costs, or whether it might update its billing methodology around the new impression reporting, according to Stagwell Media Platform’s global product managing director, Dru Sil.

“The implications are up to us to discover,” he said.

While the drop in impressions might unnerve some clients, it’s unlikely to provoke advertisers to reduce spending. Sil suggested that most advertisers will maintain spending levels, in order to establish new performance benchmarks in January and February.

“I don’t expect clients to like dramatically scale up budgets to try to get ahead of the curve. You’re likely going to continue to run what you’ve been running because you have an expected outcome that you’re trying to obtain from Amazon, regardless of the specific ad format,” said Sil.

He added: “You need to build that baseline anyway, right? And the only way to build that baseline is to be running ads.”

Benchmarking may be the real problem buyers face when they shake off the new year’s hangover.

Automated reporting processes, or media mix models that use impressions as a key input, might need to be recalibrated to account for the expected drop in reported impressions. “If you have a lot of automated processes, optimizations, reconciliations, built around these data sets already, you’re going to have to do a little bit of work,” said Paul DeJarnatt, vp and head of investment at Novus.

For most buyers, Amazon’s and Google’s tinkering with impression reporting merely underlines the importance of focusing on outcomes, rather than media KPIs, to understand campaign performance.

“The bottom line is, we don’t expect this to change campaign results. The shift will make reporting metrics look different, but it shouldn’t move ROAS or CPA, which are the outcomes our clients care about,” said Jared Smith, senior director of strategy and innovation, January Digital.

“Impressions, CPMs, they shouldn’t be north star metrics,” said Ernie DeColte, svp of media at indie agency Level. “They’re tool metrics we use to optimize towards business impact. This might be a wake-up call to a few advertisers. Maybe it’s time to think about buying differently.”

Still, communicating this change to clients who might be alarmed when they see impression counts fall off a cliff (or CPMs spike) is something media buyers across the industry are attempting to get ahead of.

“The client, even though that metric is misleading, is used to seeing a big number,” said Ladd.

“They’re used to seeing really low CPMs. They’re used to seeing really great impression volume, and that change and that difference is going to require agencies and media experts to really think about the way that they present success to the client,” she added.

Just because it’s got a donut graph doesn’t mean a report is saying very much. According to an Experian survey of 400 marketers, the profusion of dashboards and data isn’t helping marketers back up their decisions.

“In the past, a company like Unilever, buying big media in Brazil from TV Globo, had a significant competitive advantage. Now you are buying from Meta or from Google or from Amazon or from Walmart or from TikTok, and that model doesn’t favor a scale of purchase. It favors the quality of engagement you generate on the platform.”

—Unilever CEO Fernando Fernandez, speaking during its Capital Markets Day last week, on why better creative could be the secret to making its marketing operation work harder.

Local sports rights have gotten more complex and confusing as the regional sports network business changed. The leagues are now looking to simplify that offering.

As AI automates advertising workflows, the contest is shifting to who can make the decisions that deliver results.

You will be accountable for the pipeline of ideas, the speed and rigour with which they are tested, and the evidence behind every go / no-go recommendation.

This is a hands-on lead role, not pure people management: roughly 50% discovery and leadership (customer conversations, scoping, prioritisation, coaching, reporting to the CPO) and 50% building (prototypes, spikes, design and code review, demo stands). You will not be the team's only builder, but you must be able to build a credible prototype yourself and hold a technical opinion about every part of it.

You don't need to arrive as an expert in web hosting or security. If you have taken a product from nothing to its first paying customers before — as a founder, an early engineer, or the lead of an incubation team — and you get deep into unfamiliar technical territory fast, we will teach you the market.

The innovation team sits across CloudLinux and Imunify and owns the product concepts that do not yet have a home in an established product line. Ideas come from customer conversations, industry events, telemetry across more than 80,000 servers and the CPO’s strategy; the team’s job is to turn them into something a customer will pay for within a quarter, using AI coding agents throughout.

We evaluate engineers partly on how effectively they work with coding agents, and in the innovation team this is the main lever on speed. As the lead you model and coach it: prompt specificity, review quality on agent-generated code, context provision, iteration and error recovery, and end-to-end task completion. Expect to use agents to build prototypes, generate test corpora and draft customer-facing material.

#7344. What it will take for CMOs to reach the next frontier of AI-driven growth

Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit

CMOs at the largest enterprise brands across consumer goods, financial services, B2B and more are all struggling with the same thing: more AI technology has not translated into more business growth. They’re stuck chasing efficiency gains, funding tools that optimize tasks inside functional silos, running pilots that go nowhere and delegating AI decisions to IT teams.

But a few CMOs are doing it differently. Eric Schwartz, CMO of The Clorox Company, told me his marketers are building AI systems that produce highly optimized product content. They’re encoding brand voice, compliance guardrails and seasonal context into agents that work across every brand in their portfolio. Their goal isn’t to save time on doing what human writers can already do. Instead, they want to codify, scale and orchestrate the expertise that increases relevance, engagement and conversion with consumers. That’s a growth play.

This is an operating-model decision that the CMO has to own: give marketers the strategic, system-building work and shift execution to AI agents. That takes much more than a chatbot built for a solo work experience.

“I tell everyone that tries to pitch me about AI capabilities that the last thing I need is a 14th chatbot to save our marketers time,” Schwartz said. “What I need is interoperable functionality.”

Schwartz isn’t alone. A vanguard of marketers are charting the frontier of AI-native marketing. To do this requires three fundamental shifts.

Employees are becoming more efficient with AI, but report that leaders aren’t asking them to reinvest the productivity gains into strategic work; they’re just expected to produce more output. Boston Consulting Group found that 66% of frontline employees receive limited or no guidance on using saved time, and more than half don’t reinvest it into strategic work.

Measuring AI success solely on efficiency invites efficiency’s reward: a smaller budget.

For example, one CMO’s AI-powered content system is saving the company 500 hours a month. But the company’s CFO saw the dashboard and asked: “If marketing can do this with 500 fewer hours, why does the budget stay the same?” The dashboard was supposed to prove value. Instead, it made the case for a cut.

A marketing team at a regulated financial services company chose a different approach. The team was losing 360 hours a week to legal review bottlenecks, manual multi-channel content creation and constant product updates across 800-plus references. The team built a system with compliance encoded into the workflow and distribution automated across 25 channels. The result: 360 hours freed up weekly, 90% less editing time and zero agency spend.

The marketing team reinvested those hours into producing an award-winning ad campaign, not producing more of the same content. In a category where most consumers can’t name three financial lenders, breaking through the sameness drove brand recall, pipeline and market share. The system handled the production, but the humans did the work that won.

The AI opportunity isn’t time saved. Frontier CMOs reinvest that time in architecture, curation and orchestration: designing agentic workflows, encoding brand voice and steering the system to drive growth. The humans who know best what makes their brand different turn saved time into a real advantage.

Historically, marketing and revenue have operated on separate tracks. In B2B, marketing fills the top of the funnel and hands off to sales. In consumer brands, marketing creates content while commerce manages the shelf. In financial services, brand marketing and the advisors who own the relationship rarely connect. In most organizations, no single team owns the moments that decide the sale.

Sixty-seven percent of B2B buyers now prefer a rep-free experience, according to data from Gartner. Consumers and bank customers are doing their own research too. In financial services, buyers are asking AI tools for recommendations before they ever talk to an advisor. These buyers aren’t waiting for a handoff.At the frontier, there are no handoffs. AI agents carry customer data, market signals and brand and compliance context between marketing and revenue teams in real time. Context doesn’t die at a cross-functional boundary. It compounds.

Schwartz described what this looks like at Clorox. The company’s media ecosystem spans retail media, e-commerce and traditional retail, and the goal is to connect performance back to sales — or to the signals that point to sales. Most marketing organizations stop at creating and deploying campaigns. Schwartz wants that signal flowing back to show where to lean in and scale and to shape what gets created next. By closing that loop, a media budget compounds into growth instead of disappearing.

A CMO recently told me his organization has 40 active pilots, all marked green. Everything worked in the lab, but nothing survived contact with the organization. IT loved the tools, but marketing couldn’t use them.

This happens when AI adoption is delegated to IT. The CMO sponsors the budget but doesn’t own the transformation. In Writer’s 2026 survey, more than half of CMOs (52.3%) reported “significant knowledge gaps” about AI. Gartner predicts that by 2027, lack of AI literacy will rank among the top three reasons CMOs are replaced.

At the frontier, the CMO owns the entire marketing AI agenda: selecting tools, redesigning workflows and deciding what should remain human-led. That means making AI adoption a cultural shift, not a software rollout. And that can’t be delegated.

Schwartz is an example of what this looks like in practice. He made AI adoption his own rather than delegating it to an innovation team or task force.

The CMOs making progress are changing how the work gets done, moving from traditional marketing operations toward a new model of driving growth with AI. They aren’t simply doing the same work with AI layered on top, but reimagining foundational structures, systems and strategies for a new era of marketing. The frontier isn’t a place a CMO arrives at. It’s the way a CMO operates.Partner insights from Writer

If it seems like holiday ads came earlier this year, that’s because they did.

According to Nielsen, there were six times more holiday ads this September than five years ago and 11% more compared to 2025. Retailers accounted for most of the early start, airing nearly 64% of holiday ads in October, though the sector accounted for only 45% of all holiday ad spend over the past five years, per Nielsen.

The return on holiday ads can be significant. Historically, they’ve outperformed non-holiday ads in Nielsen sales lift studies of connected TV campaigns. Cosmetics holiday ads produced 3.2 times greater sales lift than non-holiday ads, with retail and restaurant holiday ads outperforming non-holiday ones by 2.4

يجب أن تكون قادراً على الجلوس أو الوقوف أمام المكتب لفترات طويلة أثناء العمل على جهاز الحاسوب.

يتراوح نطاق الأجر لهذا المنصب ما بين 110,000 و128,560 درهماً إماراتياً سنوياً. وسيتم تحديد قيمة التعويضات وفقاً لمعدلات السوق المحلية السائدة والمتطلبات القانونية المعمول بها. وفي الحالات التي يقتضيها القانون الساري، سيتم تزويد المرشحين بمعلومات نطاق الراتب خلال عملية التوظيف أو بناءً على طلبهم.

تُقدَّم المزايا وفقاً لقانون العمل الإماراتي، وتشمل الإجازة السنوية، والعطلات الرسمية، والتأمين الصحي الإلزامي، ومكافأة نهاية الخدمة. وسيتم تقديم تفاصيل إضافية خلال مرحلة تقديم العرض.

نحن جهة توظيف تكفل تكافؤ الفرص، ونلتزم بممارسات توظيف عادلة وشفافة وقائمة على الجدارة. سيتم النظر في طلبات التوظيف المقدمة من جميع المتقدمين المؤهلين دون أي تمييز يستند إلى العمر، أو الجنس، أو الهوية الجندرية أو التعبير عنها، أو التوجه الجنسي، أو العرق، أو اللون، أو الأصل الإثني، أو الجنسية، أو الدين أو المعتقد، أو الإعاقة، أو حالة الحمل أو الوضع الأبوي، أو الحالة الاجتماعية أو الأسرية، أو الوضع العسكري أو وضع المحاربين القدامى، أو الخلفية الاجتماعية والاقتصادية، أو المعلومات الجينية، أو أي خصائص أخرى يحميها القانون المحلي أو الوطني أو الدولي المعمول به.

نحن ملتزمون بتوفير عملية توظيف شاملة وميسرة للجميع. إذا كنت بحاجة إلى أي تسهيلات أو تعديلات في أي مرحلة من مراحل عملية التوظيف بسبب إعاقة أو لأي سبب آخر، يرجى التواصل معنا عبر البريد الإلكتروني [email protected]، وسنعمل معك لتلبية احتياجاتك.

تلتزم شركة ComPsych Corporation وشركاتها التابعة بالتعامل مع بياناتك الشخصية بمسؤولية وشفافية. سيتم استخدام المعلومات التي يتم جمعها أثناء عملية التوظيف لتقييم طلبك، وحيثما ينطبق ذلك، لإعداد وإدارة عرض التوظيف المقدم إليك. ستتم معالجة بياناتك الشخصية وفقاً لقوانين الخصوصية المعمول بها في بلد إقامتك أو نطاق ولايتك القضائية، والتي قد تشمل قانون خصوصية المستهلك في كاليفورنيا (CCPA)، واللائحة العامة لحماية البيانات في الاتحاد الأوروبي (GDPR)، وقانون حماية المعلومات الشخصية والوثائق الإلكترونية في كندا (PIPEDA) والتشريعات الإقليمية المتعلقة بالخصوصية، وغيرها من قوانين الخصوصية الوطنية أو المحلية السارية. للحصول على تفاصيل كاملة حول البيانات الشخصية التي نجمعها، وكيفية استخدامنا لها، وحقوقك بصفتك متقدماً للوظيفة، وكيفية التواصل معنا لطرح أسئلة تتعلق بالخصوصية، يرجى مراجعة إشعارات خصوصية بيانات المتقدمين ذات الصلة: "إشعار حماية البيانات للمتقدمين للوظائف في المنطقة الاقتصادية الأوروبية وسويسرا والمملكة المتحدة" و"إشعار خصوصية المتقدمين للوظائف على المستوى العالمي".

Define and track value per initiative and increment, and keep business decisions moving

Feed delivery learnings back into the reference architecture, our delivery method and Camunda's product

Solution and data architecture in an enterprise context: integrations and APIs, and the data a process and its agents need across systems

An AI-first mindset, including first experience designing and building enterprise-grade agentic solutions

Holds their own with senior stakeholders and gets decisions made

Experience in Finance or other back-office process domains and operations (P2P, Q2C)

Experience building value cases from operational data (baselines, volumes, value per increment), value engineering or benefits tracking

Experience with process intelligence or mining tools

Working knowledge of enterprise systems such as NetSuite, Salesforce or Zip

Did you dread the idea of coming to work today? Answer honestly, please.

If you said yes, and you work in marketing, you have plenty of company.

Across sectors, the survey paints a decidedly “meh” picture of how professionals feel about the office.
